Nifty ended Friday with sharp cuts amid selling pressure across the board, with consumer, IT and energy stocks dragging the markets the most. India VIX also moved back above its 200-DMA, indicating rising fear among the market participants. 
 Commenting on the technical charts, Rupak De, Senior Technical Analyst at LKP Securities, said that the setup has turned relatively cautious, with the index slipping below its 20-DMA for the first time in the past few sessions. Additionally, it has breached the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the prior up move from 24,571 to 26,341, he added. "With the index closing below the key support level of 25,500, the near-term bias appears weak, and there is potential for a decline toward the 25,000 mark in the short term. On the upside, immediate resistance is seen around 25,800," De said.
Here are 2 stock recommendations for Friday:
 Buy Kirloskar Oil Engines at Rs 1,375-1,385 | Upside: 5% | Target: Rs 1,500 | Stop Loss: Rs 1,320
 Kirloskar Oil Engines is currently taking a breakout of the rounding bottom formation on the daily time frame. The RSI is trending upward, reflecting positive momentum, and the stock finds support at the 21-day EMA, with all key EMAs rising. The stock is trading above important moving averages, indicating a bullish trend. 1,320 could work as an immediate support, and a hurdle can be seen at 1,500.
 (Drumil Vithlani, Technical Research Analyst, Bonanza Portfolio)

 Bajaj Finance is currently taking a breakout of the downward-moving channel on the daily time frame. Momentum Indicator RSI is trading near the overbought region, which confirms the bullishness in the script.

As preparations for the Union Budget 2026–27 gather pace, the groundwork underway signals a clear policy intent to accelerate domestic demand, revive private investment and generate employment, according to a budget note by Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL). The brokerage has identified five stocks across auto, agriculture, defence, financials and infrastructure themes, which it believes could deliver strong gains for investors.
 "The Budget is expected to focus on income-tax, GST, and customs simplification to enhance ease of doing business and support fiscal consolidation, alongside targeted support for agriculture, MSMEs, manufacturing, infrastructure, higher defence capex, EVs, and renewables through credit and incentives," the note authored by Research Analysts Sneha Poddar and Rekha Jaat said.
A strong capital expenditure thrust across highways, logistics, defence, rail freight corridors and connectivity is anticipated, complemented by emphasis on skilling, rural prosperity, women empowerment, AI adoption, climate action and digital finance to anchor India’s next phase of economic expansion, the note added.
The finance ministry started work on the Union Budget for 2026-27 from October 9 as per a circular issued by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA).
The preparations come against the backdrop of an additional 50% US tariff on most Indian goods and other external headwinds. These have raised risks to India's growth and jobs outlook, prompting calls for stronger support to the export sector.
 Live Events
 5 stocks to buy: 
The stocks recommended by MOFSL are TVS Motor Company, UPL , Bharat Dynamics (BDL), M&M Financial Services and Dalmia Bharat , and each of these stocks has been assigned a 20% weight.
 1) TVS Motors: TVS Motors continues to outperform peers and is well-positioned to benefit from the budget’s push to boost domestic consumption and rural demand through higher allocations, income support, and infrastructure spending.
MOFSL said that improving rural sentiment, strong entry-level recovery and sustained two-wheeler demand will be key triggers. Moreover, the company's market share gains, easing discounts, and margin expansion will provide strong earnings visibility. The Apache and Ntorq maker remains its top pick in OEMs.
 2) UPL: The diversified agrochemical leader is well positioned to benefit from the union budget push riding on rural prosperity via higher agri credit, MSME support, and value-chain strengthening, lifting farmer incomes and crop-protection demand.
The company's strong points are stronger volumes, export tailwinds, improved working-capital discipline and post-bond-repayment balance-sheet strength, the brokerage note said. The company's rising focus on speciality chemicals supports solid 2HFY26 growth.
 3) Bharat Dynamics: Bharat Dynamics (BDL), a defence play, has a robust Rs 50,000 crore order pipeline over five years, with Rs 20,000 crore targeted in 2-3 years. This aligns with the expected defence capex surge and infra push.
The recent Rs 2.5 lakh crore DAC approvals for missiles, undersea warfare, and naval arms leverage BDL's tactical/strategic expertise, propelling FY31 turnover to Rs 100bn via indigenisation and lower provisions, the note said.
 4) M&M Financial Services: M&M Financial is poised for Union Budget 2026-27 benefits via rural prosperity, MSME credit, and employment focus, driving PV/tractor loan growth amid surging volumes from festive demand, GST cuts, and restocking.
The company targets Rs 3 lakh crore in assets under management (AUM) by 2030, which is at an 18-20% CAGR, bolstered by AI underwriting, lower credit costs, controlled opex, and margin stability for strong earnings visibility in retail portfolios.
 5) Dalmia Bharat: The cement company benefits from the budget’s infra capex surge, PMAY rural housing, and urban projects, driving cement volume growth.
Dalmia Bharat is a low-cost cement producer with high blending ratios, green power and low freight. The company is targeting 62 mtpa capacity by FY28, and its cost optimisation endeavours will likely lift EBITDA margins amid sector consolidation.

Reliance Power 's board of directors on Monday approved the issuance of up to 46.20 crore equity shares/warrants worth Rs 1,525 crore via preferential allotment mode.
 The board has set the issue price at Rs 33 per share.
The issue price of equity shares/warrants is at a discount of 13% over Monday's closing price of Rs 38.15 on the NSE. The announcement was made after market hours and Reliance Power shares on Monday ended with gains of Rs 1.81 or 4.98% over the previous closing price.
 Reliance Infrastructure Limited, the promoter of the company, will enhance its equity stake by over Rs 600 crore, a company filing said. The other investors in the preferential issue are Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited and Sanatan Financial Advisory Services Private Limited.
The proceeds from the preferential issue will be utilised to expand business operations directly and/or through investment in subsidiaries and joint ventures, debt reduction and for general corporate purposes, the filing said.

The markets worldwide are waiting with bated breath on what will be a historic policy announcement from the US Federal Reserve , where the central bank is expected to usher in a rate cut cycle.
 The announcement will be made at 11:30 pm IST (Indian Standard Time) on Wednesday.
If analysts are to be believed, the US Fed is all but certain to cut interest rates for the first time in more than four years.
However, there is no consensus on the quantum of reduction. Some are predicting a smaller cut of a quarter of a percentage point, while others believe a bigger half-point reduction is in the works.
Senior officials at the US central bank, including Powell, have indicated that a rate cut is coming, as inflation eases toward the bank's long-term target of 2%, and the labour market continues to cool in the post-Covid economy.
 Live Events
If the Fed starts the rate cut cycle, the Reserve Bank of India is also expected to follow suit.
A smaller cut would be a more predictable move, while a bigger cut would do more to boost demand — while also running the risk of reigniting inflation.
 WATCH LIVE TODAY: Press conference with #FOMC Chair Powell at 2:30 p.m. ET: https://t.co/1uJrua5qsH https://t.co/FJa6TbkDMt pic.twitter.com/87g5NJITsz 
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) September 18, 2024 
By the end 2024, markets are expecting a total reduction of at least 100 basis points in the first rate cut cycle in over 4 years since 2020.
But whether the Fed goes for 25 or 50 bps, the biggest trigger for stock prices to move up or down would be Powell's motivation behind the cut.
Asset classes from stocks, currencies and fixed income could all log swings in the immediate aftermath of the Fed decision.
While easing US interest rates are directionally positive for equities in general, “we should keep in mind interest rates are just one variable in a complex adaptive system that determines the direction of Indian equity markets”, said Anoop Vijaykumar, Investments and Head of Research at Capitalmind.

docs.title: Stock recommendations for 26 October from MarketSmith India
docs.text:
Markets 
 Stock recommendations for 26 October from MarketSmith India
 MarketSmith India 6 min read 26 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 MarketSmith India reveals its top stock recommendations for today, 26 October. Get expert insights into the best-performing stocks to guide your investment decisions. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Stock market recap : Indian equities extended their losing streak to a fourth straight session on Friday, as crude oil prices nearing $114 per barrel, renewed foreign selling, and a global selloff in technology stocks weighed on sentiment. Nifty 50 fell 87.65 points, or 0.39%, to close at 22,600, after sliding to an intraday low of 22,372, while Sensex slipped 125.56 points, or 0.17%, to settle at 73,123.83.
 Both indices recovered sharply from the day's lows in the afternoon, led by IT stocks. For the week, Nifty lost about 2.4%. IT was the best-performing sector, with TCS, Infosys, HCL Tech, and Tech Mahindra rising, as investors bought Indian software firms despite overnight losses in U.S. tech giants such as Meta and Nvidia. Metals and Realty were the weakest sectors, with Tata Steel and Hindalco falling about 3% each, while Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, Jio Financial Services, and NTPC also declined.
 The Bank Nifty fell 1.16%. Selling was far heavier in midcap and smallcap stocks, and breadth was deeply negative, with only 624 stocks advancing, 3,011 stocks declining, and 89 remaining unchanged. Crude oil, foreign flows, and quarterly earnings will remain in focus next week.
 Two stock recommendations by MarketSmith India:
 Buy: Garware Hi-Tech Films Limited (current price: ₹ 7040) 
 Why it’s recommended: Strong demand for high-margin specialty films such as Paint Protection Films (PPF), solar control and architectural films, supported by ongoing capacity expansion and backward integration initiatives. Increasing export footprint and premiumization of product portfolio, with specialty films contributing a growing share of revenue and driving margin expansion. 
 Key metrics: P/E: 36.31, 52-week high: ₹ 7,990.00, volume: ₹ 169.43 crore 
 Technical analysis: Reclaimed its 200-EMA 
 Risk factors: High dependence on global markets and export revenues exposes the company to tariff changes, trade restrictions, currency fluctuations, and overseas demand slowdowns. Raw material price volatility and rising competition from global film manufacturers could pressure margins and market share. 
 Buy: ₹ 6,970-7,075 
 Target price: ₹ 8,200 in two to three months 
 Stop loss: ₹ 6,500 
 Buy: Nazara Technologies Limited (current price: ₹ 402)
 Why it’s recommended: Expansion of its global gaming platform through acquisitions, proprietary gaming IPs, and strong growth in businesses such as Kiddopia, Fusebox Games, and Animal Jam. Benefiting from the rapid growth of the gaming and esports industry, supported by improving monetization, operating leverage, and AI/data-driven user acquisition capabilities. 
 Key metrics: P/E: 17.10, 52-week high: ₹ 419.90, volume: ₹ 128.41 crore 
 Technical analysis: Bounced from its 50-EMA 
 Risk factors: Acquisition-led growth strategy increases integration, execution, and capital allocation risks, particularly with large overseas transactions. Gaming revenues are dependent on the sustained popularity of key titles/IPs and are exposed to changing consumer preferences and platform policies. 
 Buy at: ₹ 398–404 
 Target price: ₹ 480 in two to three months 
 Stop loss: ₹ 373 
 How the Nifty 50 performed on 23 October 
 Indian equity markets ended Friday's session on a weak note, with Nifty 50 declining 87.65 points (0.39%) to 22,600.00, compared with its previous close of 22,687.65. The benchmark opened at 22,742.20, touched an intraday high of 22,787.25, and fell to a low of 22,372.00 before recovering sharply from lower levels. Selling pressure was broad-based across sectors, led by Nifty Metal (-2.71%), Consumer Durables (-2.63%), Realty (-2.38%), and PSU Bank (-2.26%), while IT (-0.27%) and Auto (-0.60%) demonstrated relative resilience. Overall market breadth remained decisively negative, with 624 stocks advancing, 3,011 stocks declining, and 89 remaining unchanged. This translates into an advance-decline ratio of approximately 1:4.8, indicating widespread selling pressure beyond the benchmark index.
 The index formed a bearish daily candle with a pronounced lower shadow, reflecting buying interest at intraday lows, although selling pressure at higher levels remains evident. Price action continues to follow a pattern of lower-highs and lower-lows, reinforcing the prevailing downtrend. The index remains below its key moving averages, while the broader descending trendline continues to indicate sustained bearish sentiment. The Relative Strength Index (RSI) stands at 42.38, below the neutral 50 mark, suggesting weak momentum despite its recovery from oversold territory. Meanwhile, the MACD remains in negative territory, with the MACD line (-169.46) above the signal line (-222.63) and a positive histogram of 53.17, indicating improving short-term momentum.

Initial festive-season registrations since Navratri have been mixed. Commercial vehicle (CV) registrations grew 21% year-on-year (YoY), while two-wheeler (2W) registrations rose 13%. Dealer checks across Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand indicate moderating demand due to a high base following last year's GST cuts, intermittent weakness in rural demand, and longer waiting periods, particularly for passenger vehicles. Meanwhile, electric vehicle (EV) adoption continues to grow at a robust double-digit pace across segments. A Bihar dealer expects Honda's two-wheeler sales to grow 15–18% during the festive period, below the 24% growth recorded between April and August 2026. For Hero MotoCorp, a Jharkhand dealer expects festive-season growth of 10%, compared with 12% in the first half of FY27. Rural demand is likely to remain healthy in the state due to normal rainfall. Nuvama's checks with passenger-vehicle dealers in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar also indicate uneven festive demand. docs.title: Viral investment tip? SEBI urges investors to check these 3 things before trusting online advice or making payments
docs.text:
Still, before proceeding with any such investment ideas, it is prudent for well-informed investors to be cautious and verify any tips or freely available information. This is because a seemingly lucrative and harmless investment opportunity or idea may not always be genuine or provide the promised results. 
 Furthermore, transferring any money without proper background verification, risk assessment, and confirmation of the real recipient of the funds can expose investors to financial fraud and cause regret later on. 
 To help seasoned and new investors make meaningful, informed investment decisions, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has highlighted three key checks through its investor awareness initiative, ‘ Samajh Se Investing Simple.’ 
 In this initiative, the focus is on understanding investments at a conceptual level, verifying an intermediary’s registration, downloading trading applications with a clearly defined, verified label, and checking payment details before transferring funds. This message has been sent to citizens' WhatsApp numbers to raise awareness. 
 "The investment tip is viral. But is it legit? 
 Before you trust the tip, check the facts. 
 • Intermediary? Check for SEBI registration. 
 • Trading app? Download Apps with Verified Label 
 • Investment payment? Use SEBI Check Tool before making payment 
 An investor awareness initiative by SEBI. 
 For more information and verified resources, visit investor.sebi.gov.in/ssis or download SEBI Saa ₹ thi App." 
 To ensure complete financial protection, before following any investment tip or advice or dealing with a market intermediary, it is prudent for investors to carefully verify the intermediary’s SEBI registration status through official sources. The verification of registration can help investors avoid unauthorised and fraudulent entities posing as fair and legitimate market professionals and participants. 
 When you are looking to download trading applications, they should be obtained only from official sources, such as the Google Play Store and the Apple App Store. APK files sent in random messages, or links sent via email, WhatsApp, etc., should not be clicked or used to download any application. This makes it critical for investors to check for verified applications from official app stores and confirm their authenticity before trusting them blindly and falling prey to fraudulent schemes. 
 Finally, before making any investment-related payment, investors should use SEBI’s ‘Check tool’ to analyse, verify, and review the relevant payment details. This simple yet meaningful step can help investors identify suspicious payment requests before funds are transferred to other accounts. 
 In summary, a viral investment tip should never replace prudence and independent verification of facts. All investors should therefore stay vigilant, check the source, confirm its authenticity and verify payment details before committing their funds. A few simple yet meaningful steps can go a long way toward helping investors protect their savings and make more informed investment decisions. 
 If you have any complaints regarding malpractice in the equity markets, you can refer to the official SEBI website at the following link: https://www.sebi.gov.in/ and click on the ‘Vigilance tab ’. Under this tab, you will find the option to ‘Register a complaint’ 
You can submit your complaint using these simple steps to ensure your financial well-being remains intact and that you are protected from unwanted messages, threats, and potential financial losses at all times.

docs.title: Why fund managers are mixed on gilt funds
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Why fund managers are mixed on gilt funds
 Jash Kriplani 8 min read 25 Oct 2026, 02:57 PM IST 
 Summary
 Rising yields offer an opportunity to lock in higher yields, but inflation risks, higher crude prices and further rate hikes could push bond yields higher. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Bond yields are climbing globally, and Indian investors in gilt funds face a difficult choice: lock in higher yields now or wait for a potentially better entry point.
 The US 10-year Treasury yield is hovering around 5%, up from around 4% a year ago, while Brent crude oil has climbed past $110 a barrel on supply concerns in West Asia, raising the risk that inflation will stay higher for longer.
 In India, yield on the benchmark 10-year government security (g-sec) stood at 7.47% on 23 October, up from around 6.76% in mid-August and about 6.54% a year ago. The yield is at its highest level in three-and-a-half years. Rising US yields, higher crude oil prices and monetary tightening at home have all contributed to the pressure.
 For investors, rising yields cut both ways. Higher yields can make government bonds more attractive to new investors, but they also push down the prices of existing bonds, inflicting mark-to-market losses on debt funds that hold them. Gilt funds, which invest predominantly in government securities, can be particularly sensitive to these moves when their portfolios have longer durations.
 On average, gilt funds’ net asset values (NAVs) have fallen about 2.5% since mid-August. Some fund managers see the correction as an opportunity to build positions gradually. Others believe yields could rise further, making patience the better strategy.
 The case for gilt funds 
 The argument for investing now rests on the view that yields are already attractive and that much of the expected monetary tightening may be reflected in bond prices.
 “Yields at close to 7.45-7.5% are a good entry point. But investors should enter in a staggered manner and not put the entire sum in at one go, as oil is rising and yields are elevated globally. We don’t know where the top will be,” said Puneet Pal, head of fixed income at PGIM India Mutual Fund.
 Marzban Irani, executive director-investments at LIC MF, said yields had risen and absolute levels were attractive for starting to build a position.
 Joydeep Sen, corporate trainer and author, pointed to the gap between bond yields and the policy rate as a reason to believe that further increases in the 10-year yield could be limited.
 “Over the last 25 years, the average spread between the repo rate and the 10-year g-sec yield has been about one percentage point. Today, it is almost double that. So even if the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) hikes further, the 10-year yield may not move up as much, since it is already in an elevated zone,” he said. He too favours a staggered approach.
 On 7 October, the RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points (bps) to 5.5% and changed its stance to “calibrated tightening”.
 Bond prices and yields move inversely. When yields rise, existing bonds with lower coupons become less valuable, leading to mark-to-market losses for debt funds. Longer-duration portfolios are more exposed to such losses because their bond prices are more sensitive to interest-rate changes.
 “Staying invested for a period close to a fund’s duration, typically over a seven-to-nine-year horizon can help to reduce the impact of volatility. When your holding period is longer, the effects of interest rate movements largely cancel out. If yields rise, the fund’s NAV falls in the short term, but the fund reinvests its interest income and maturing bonds at the higher yields, which makes up for that loss over time. So, your return ends up close to the yield at which you entered. And if yield levels normalize, you also stand to benefit from capital appreciation. Yield of close to 7.5% is a good level to lock-in for investors with a longer investment horizon,” said Ashish Chadha, a registered investment advisor.
 Historical returns offer some support for the long-term case. A Mint analysis of gilt funds since 2005 showed that no five-year holding period or longer delivered a negative return. The minimum return rose to 3.3% over seven years and 4.5% over 10 years, while average returns remained between 7.2% and 7.8% across holding periods ranging from one year to 10 years. The maximum return was 11.9% over seven years and 10.4% over 10 years.
 Fund houses are also finding opportunities across the debt market, not just in long-duration government bonds.
 “We find the entire basket of debt funds attractive due to higher yields and duration opportunities. Accordingly, we recommend the long-duration g-secs and state government securities for duration, and we suggest the 2-5 year corporate bond space for capturing accruals,” ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund said in its outlook note.
 Sushil Budhia, senior fund manager-fixed income at Nippon India Mutual Fund, believes much of the negative news is already priced in.
 “With the RBI changing its stance to calibrated tightening, we expect three more 25-bps-hikes from hereon, taking the repo rate to about 6.25%. A large part of this rate hike cycle is already built into the current ten-year yield. Yields may remain in a narrow corridor of 15-20 basis points and not move too much either way from here,” he said.
 The case for caution 
 Not everyone believes the current yield is an attractive enough entry point. Some fund managers expect yields to rise further before stabilising, potentially giving investors a better opportunity to invest.
 “Yields have gone up quickly. You may see a retracement if at all of 10-15 bps to 7.30%, but it may not sustain there. A lot of issues need to be sorted out before yields can come down meaningfully,” said Shantanu Godambe, fund manager at DSP Mutual Fund.

docs.title: Fell for a fake trading app or guaranteed-return WhatsApp group? What to do immediately? Can you recover your money?
docs.text:
WhatsApp and Telegram groups are often used to build a false sense of trust through fake profit screenshots and stock tips, before members are directed to fraudulent trading apps that can drain their savings. According to data from Ministry of Finance, as many as 235 lakh of demat accounts were added during FY 2026 (till December 2025), pushing the total count beyond 21.6 crore. The mutual fund industry also continued to expand, with 5.9 crore unique investors recorded at the same period, of which 3.5 crore (as of November 2025) were from non-tier-I and tier-II cities. The rising scams prompted the Securities and Exchange Board of India ( Sebi ) to issue an advisory warning investors against WhatsApp stock-tip groups that use fraudulent tactics to create a false impression of credibility and lure investors. In a statement on Thursday, the market regulator said that certain unregistered persons were offering stock recommendations to investors through invitation-only WhatsApp groups under the guise of free investor education. These operators often use overseas numbers posing as market experts. "To make these calls look credible, certain members, acting in concert with the operators, post false claims of profit and praise the 'expert'. This practice, known as astroturfing, creates a false impression of genuine support and induces unsuspecting investors to act on the call," Sebi said. If you already fell for a fake trading app or guaranteed-return WhatsApp group and lost money, recovery may be possible if you act quickly. According to a blog post by Tata Mutual Fund , a fraud victim should immediately contact their bank or payment provider, call the national cybercrime helpline at 1930, and lodge a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. Prompt reporting can improve the chances of blocking or tracing the funds before they are withdrawn or transferred further, although recovery is not guaranteed. However, you cannot force a refund or sue a broker or company just because a stock recommendation or tip went bad. This is why consulting a Sebi-registered investment advisor can be a prudent approach for making investments. In January last year, Sebi introduced restrictions on how finfluencers can provide stock-related content under the guise of investor education on social media. Stock prices used for educational purposes must be at least three months old, and live stock prices cannot be used. Registered entities are also prohibited from paying influencers for any direct or indirect association'. Here are some more tips, as per the blog post, that may help you avoid fake apps and WhatsApp investment scams in India: — Treat ‘guaranteed return’ claims as a warning sign: Markets are volatile and mostly unpredictable in nature, so anyone promising you guaranteed returns or saying that they could double or triple your investment money in short time must be treated as a potential scam. Remember that as per Sebi guidelines, legitimate investment platforms and apps cannot promise assured returns. — Stay away from investment advice shared on WhatsApp groups: Scammers often use WhatsApp to pose as market experts and run guaranteed return scams in India. Be wary of the links shared on WhatsApp groups as these links can be phishing scams that can empty your bank account. — Always verify credentials Don’t take investment advice from individuals or platforms without verifying their registration status as only Sebi-registered investment advisers can offer investment advice to clients. — Check if the app is legitimate: Before you start investing through a trading or investment app, check if they have Sebi's ‘verified’ badge on your phone's app store. You can also go to the investor support page on Sebi's website and check the list of Sebi-authorised intermediary apps. Disclaimer: This story is for educational purposes only. docs.title: Eleven hours of Trump: what we saw on the ground at seven rallies in seven days
docs.text:
Global 
 Eleven hours of Trump: what we saw on the ground at seven rallies in seven days
 Philip Wegmann , Natalie Andrews , Alex Leary , The Wall Street Journal 8 min read 26 Oct 2026, 06:55 AM IST 
 Summary
 The blitz of visits to largely red states aims to stem GOP losses by motivating Trump supporters to show up on Election Day. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Joe Douglas knew what to expect when he drove 90 minutes to see President Trump in Wichita, Kan., this week. “I’ve heard everything he is going to say,” the 70-year-old retired pipeline worker said, sporting the red MAGA hat he bought in 2016.
 So why make the drive? “Because this is live,” Douglas said Monday, adding that he had never seen the president, whom he voted for in the past three elections, in person.
 Trump has returned to the rally stage in force, hoping to energize his supporters and defy the polls predicting deep Republican losses in November. Crowds are generally smaller than they were when he was on the ballot, but the president is reveling in the attention, touting his agenda, stirring the pot and veering off script.
 President Trump headlined seven campaign rallies in a week, hoping to boost voter turnout for the midterm elections. Photo: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters
 Some Republicans fear the spectacle will motivate Democrats and give his opponents plenty of fodder to paint the president as out of touch. But at the arenas, gyms and airport hangars where he has been holding court, the Trump show is unabashedly back—perhaps for a final time as his decadelong dominance in politics begins to sunset.
 Wall Street Journal reporters attended every one of Trump’s midterm rallies this week: seven events across seven states, starting in Kansas on Monday and ending in Michigan on Sunday, with stops along the way in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida and Georgia. All told, Trump spoke for more than 11 hours. By Saturday, his voice was noticeably hoarse.
 Here’s what we learned:
 All about Trump
 The rallies are something of a security blanket for Trump, according to advisers, freeing him from the pressures of the job, critical news coverage and the lowest approval rating of any president heading into midterm elections in Wall Street Journal polling dating to the 1990s. Most analysts expect the GOP will lose control of the House and possibly the Senate.
 But on stage, Trump is met with cheering crowds and fleeting signs of opposition. In Sioux City, Iowa, congressional candidate Joe Mitchell lamented Trump hasn’t been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize and presented him with a framed “man of the century” certificate. Trump pauses at rallies to play a video clip of a CNN analyst explaining that among Republican voters, he is far more popular than Ronald Reagan or Abraham Lincoln.
 Throughout the week, Trump addressed critics who allege that he is slipping by returning to one of his favorite topics: the mental acuity test that he says he aced: “I know everything that I’m doing,” he told a crowd in South Carolina.
 Trump also said no fewer than 10 times in Wichita that “nobody appreciates me” despite what he considers his many accomplishments, a routine that culminated in a story he told about expressing that sentiment to a group of businessmen at the White House. “And then I look up and I say, ‘Oh, wait…is this the Oval Office that we’re in?…That means I’m president.”
 Few things annoy Trump more than a small crowd. Friday in Fort Myers, Fla., he marveled at a packed arena on a college campus and claimed the crowd outside was “10 miles long.” There were a large number of people outside, but the line didn’t stretch for 10 miles. At every rally he points out how many cameras are in the back of the room. “Oh, wow, that’s a lot of fake news,” he said in North Carolina to laughter and boos.
 A midterms strategy
 Critics see self-aggrandizement, a blizzard of falsehoods and increasingly uncivil attacks on his opponents. But there is a strategy behind putting Trump at the center of the midterms. Advisers see Trump as the single best motivator for voters.
 The Trump political machine is rerunning much of the playbook that returned him to the Oval Office in 2024: targeting the MAGA base, especially low-propensity voters, in red states. A senior White House official said that despite Trump’s polarizing nature, the approach is paying dividends, pointing to Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has seen an uptick in enthusiasm in internal metrics.
 Still, it is a risky approach. Far-reaching Republican losses in the midterms could signal that Trump’s political power is diminishing. And the president has made statements at his rallies that could make life harder for vulnerable Republicans.
 Saturday night in Georgia, Trump bragged that oil revenues in the U.S. are surging because of the conflict in the Middle East. He said that his advisers told him not to say that because people are paying more for gasoline. “But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn, I’m gonna say it: We’re making a freaking fortune.’ Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are gonna come down,” Trump said.
 Some longtime political allies wonder if the grueling pace is getting to the 80-year-old president. Mike Lindell, a businessman and longtime friend of the president’s, said during a recent videoconference with Trump’s allies that the president “looked the tiredest I’ve ever seen him.” Lindell added, “You’ve got to realize, these rallies are just one after another after another.”
 A White House official said nonstop travel has pushed the administration to its limits, but insisted that Trump is energized. After rallies, the president has asked aides which part of his remarks they liked best, according to people involved in the conversations.

Mint Money Why your good fund feels bad Dhirendra Kumar (Value Research) 4 min read 25 Oct 2026, 07:00 AM IST Summary A fund can beat its rivals and still lose you money, but that’s not an automatic justification for selling it. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now Think of an investor who puts a large sum of money into a good equity fund a few months before a market peak. It's a well-managed fund, and in the fall that follows, it loses 18% while the index drops 24%. On any sensible basis, the fund has done well: the market has fallen sharply, but the fund manager has lost much less. When the market turns, this head start will matter. The fund needs to rise about 22% to get back to where it started; the index needs about 32%. But our investor sees none of the good news. On his screen, there’s a big red number next to the fund. The fact that it beat the index feels like a meaningless statistic. Two different yardsticks The difficulty is obvious: two different things are being compared. Judged against its benchmark, especially during a fall, any analyst would say that this fund did well. The investor’s yardstick, though, is not benchmark-relative returns but his own absolute returns. Those depend on when he invested, whether he made a lump-sum investment or used an SIP, and simply where he entered the market cycle. In my experience, his own loss drives the decision to sell, but he blames the fund to justify it. This allows the investor to ignore the responsibility he should take and shifts it to the fund manager . When the market turns, this head start will matter. The fund needs to rise about 22% to get back to where it started; the index needs about 32%. But our investor sees none of the good news. On his screen, there’s a big red number next to the fund. The fact that it beat the index feels like a meaningless statistic. Two different yardsticks The difficulty is obvious: two different things are being compared. Judged against its benchmark, especially during a fall, any analyst would say that this fund did well. The investor’s yardstick, though, is not benchmark-relative returns but his own absolute returns. Those depend on when he invested, whether he made a lump-sum investment or used an SIP, and simply where he entered the market cycle. In my experience, his own loss drives the decision to sell, but he blames the fund to justify it. This allows the investor to ignore the responsibility he should take and shifts it to the fund manager . Something similar happens when a fund that was a leader a couple of years ago becomes ordinary. Suppose a fund delivered 8% last year, but its five-year annualised returns are 18%. This kind of variation is routine in equity funds, whose track records are built on uneven years: some great, some good, some bad, and a few ugly. An investor who has stayed invested for a few years sees one dull year among many good ones. The one who arrives after the boom feels tricked into buying a fund that used to be good but has now suddenly turned bad. It's the same fund, but the two investors' experiences are the exact opposite. The reason all this matters, and why I’m explaining it in somewhat tedious detail, is that the psychology here can wreck the arithmetic. A red number on your portfolio tracker is just a paper loss until you talk yourself into selling, at which point it becomes real. Except for the occasional brief bonanza, the rewards of equity investing come from years of your own patience and consistency, along with the quality of the fund you choose. This is even more true of SIPs, where stop-start investing can seriously damage your returns. When to worry But of course, there are funds that genuinely decline. What I have said above shouldn't be taken to mean every fund should be held indefinitely, regardless of performance. The test for when to start worrying is, I admit, not that easy. The first thing to watch is how a fund performs against peers in the same category. Look over a period of a year or more, because shorter periods are subject to all kinds of random variation. Funds that perform exceptionally well for a time can slip to the middle of the performance tables. This is natural and common. But when a fund sinks towards the bottom and stays there for more than a year, it is a different situation and warrants a closer look. Another useful test is its five- and seven-year returns, which put recent problems in a longer-term context and show whether the fund still deserves patience. The same tests also protect you in the opposite situation: you could be invested in a fund that is going bad, but because of the timing of your investments, the number on the screen could still be green. A good investor should therefore apply these tests even to funds that are showing a profit. Of course, this is too much hard work to do manually and could easily become a distraction. But today, you can use tools to automate the process and let it run in the background. The colour of the number on your screen tells you about your timing, not about your fund.  Rising US Treasury yields and a weaker rupee are drawing Indian investors toward dollar-denominated debt as a fixed-income diversifier.

 Mumbai: The surge in US Treasury yields, with the 10-year touching 5.37% earlier this month, its highest since 2002, is opening another avenue for Indian investors to access the world’s largest economy. With the rupee weakening and the gap between US and Indian bond yields narrowing, experts advise considering US debt to diversify fixed-income portfolios.
 Global bond yields have been rising amid a surge in crude oil and other commodity prices, driven by the West Asia war. That is stoking inflation concerns and prompting a shift towards tighter monetary policy. The gap between 10-year US and Indian government bond yields has narrowed to around 2 percentage points. The shrinking differential is adding to the appeal of dollar-denominated debt, particularly as the rupee has depreciated 8.38% against the dollar over the 12 months to 23 October.
 Nirav Karkera, head of research and fund manager at W by Groww, said interest in US debt is building amid high US yields and a weaker rupee. Indian mutual funds investing in US Treasuries manage only about ₹ 400 crore, largely because most have stopped accepting fresh investments due to the industry’s overseas investment limits, he said.
 Nirav Karkera, head of research and fund manager at W by Groww, said interest in US debt is building amid high US yields and a weaker rupee. Indian mutual funds investing in US Treasuries manage only about ₹ 400 crore, largely because most have stopped accepting fresh investments due to the industry’s overseas investment limits, he said.
 A weaker rupee can boost returns in rupee terms. For instance, a 4-5% return in dollars on short-term US Treasuries could translate into 7.5-8% in rupee terms, before fees and taxes, assuming annual rupee depreciation of 2.5-3%.
 One alternative is to invest through the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), which allows Indian residents to remit up to $250,000 a year for permitted transactions. At Vested Finance, a global investment platform that gives Indian retail investors access to international financial markets, around 5% of investors have invested in US debt, said Viram Shah, the company’s founder and chief executive. Here is a closer look at the available routes and the considerations for investors.
 Different routes
 One option is to invest through an Indian mutual fund scheme that invests in US Treasuries or other overseas debt securities. Investors can transact in rupees without opening an overseas brokerage account, while the fund handles the investments. However, most such schemes have stopped accepting fresh subscriptions because of the industry’s overseas investment limits: $7 billion for overseas mutual fund investments and a separate $1 billion limit for overseas exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Those limits are already exhausted.
 “The more practical route today is LRS, which allows individuals to remit up to $250,000 a year for eligible overseas investments, including US Treasury securities and US-listed Treasury ETFs, while accounting for foreign-exchange conversion costs and tax collected at source (TCS),” said Karkera.
 Investors can access overseas-listed products, such as the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF and Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF, through platforms such as INDmoney and Vested Finance, subject to product availability. While this route offers a wider choice of investments, investors must factor in foreign-exchange conversion costs, brokerage charges and tax-compliance requirements, and be comfortable managing an overseas investment account.
 “GIFT City could become a convenient route for US debt as more products offering exposure to US debt are launched,” Karkera said.
 Tax considerations
 Indian debt funds purchased on or after 1 April 2023 no longer qualify for long-term capital gains treatment and are taxed at the investor’s applicable income-tax slab rate, irrespective of the holding period. Gains on US-domiciled debt ETFs, however, are subject to a different tax treatment, with long-term capital gains taxed at 12.5%.
 Shah said the tax treatment of ETFs holding US bonds depends on the product and remains unsettled in some cases. Indian tax authorities and financial experts continue to debate whether these funds should be taxed as foreign assets or as debt funds. “Tax should not be the main reason to move money into US debt,” Shah said.
 The rupee is an important determinant of returns, Shah said. A weaker rupee boosts returns in rupee terms, as it has over the past year, while a recovery in the currency can erode them. “US debt is a currency decision as much as a rate decision,” he said, adding that diversification is a stronger reason to consider US debt, given that most Indian investors hold nearly all their fixed-income assets in rupees.
 A small dollar allocation could make sense for investors who expect to spend money overseas in the next few years, such as on education or travel, Shah said. He also advised investors to favour shorter-maturity Treasuries. Longer-dated bonds are more vulnerable to price declines if yields rise further, while shorter maturities carry less interest-rate risk.

Opinion 
 Rogue Chinese bots: Why AI doesn't have to be evil to cause chaos—and why that's a global problem
 Catherine Thorbecke 4 min read 25 Oct 2026, 07:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 It turns out artificial intelligence agents going 'off-script' is not just a quirk of bots made by American firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. Agents running on China's biggest tech company's cloud server went rogue—that should tell us this is a worldwide issue. We need more openness from AI makers. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 I wrote before that it was only a matter of time before we saw ‘rogue’ behaviour from Chinese AI agents. Now, we’re starting to see what that looks like. So far, they really want to find the best way into the zoo. 
 That may sound far from our Terminator nightmares, but it’s the latest warning shot from a string of incidents involving computer systems behaving in ways we can’t anticipate or control. 
 A team of international researchers last week published findings on a “fleet” of Chinese AI agents running on a cloud platform operated by Tencent. The agents were apparently trying to answer a simple question: ‘Which entrance to Chengdu Zoo do most people use?’ 
 They attempted to get around anti-bot protections on Amap, Alibaba’s equivalent of Google Maps, including by probing protected IT systems. The researchers found no evidence that the agents accessed private systems or coordinated with each other in real time. 
 Tencent later confirmed that the activity originated from evaluations of third-party models. Some agents “exhibited unintended web-browsing behavior,” the firm said in a post on X, while emphasizing its commitment to building safe and responsible AI. 
 The researchers, an ad hoc group called Swarmchasers, most of whom met at a San Francisco hackathon, don’t believe the issues they encountered are unique to Tencent. 
 What made the case notable, they said, was that previous public examples of agentic fleets behaving this way involved US labs. Their findings indicate that this is an unsolved global problem, and that agents can “spontaneously go off script” even when performing innocuous tasks. There are likely “more undiscovered fleets all over the internet,” they warned. 
 In what it believes to be a first, the team made contact with the agents after detecting signals that the tools were aware they were being observed. The researchers invited a New York Times reporter to question the agents. They offered a mundane explanation for their motives: They were trying to answer users’ questions as accurately as possible. In other words, AI systems don’t need nefarious motives to cause chaos. They might just need a goal. 
 What I find remarkable is how much of this behaviour is being uncovered by loosely organized hobbyists rather than the makers of these tools. AI firms shouldn’t leave that job to outsiders. They need to invest more into discovering, tracking and disclosing what their agents are up to. 
 This has become especially urgent since the Hugging Face incident, which spurred a heated debate about the language used to describe AI that can act on its own. There’s a balance to strike. Jargon can make serious incidents seem inaccessible. But ascribing human motives to AI feeds an already overheated hype cycle and shifts responsibility for bad behaviour away from the people who build and deploy these tools. 
 Even the word “rogue” has become fuzzy. Rowan Howard-Jones, one of the authors of the Tencent report, acknowledged that grey area. She roughly defines rogue behaviour as an agent acting outside the bounds of a task, often using third-party sites to do so. “If I ask an agent to check my bank account balance, but I forget to give the agent my authentication details, the outcome shouldn’t be the agent hacking into my bank,” she told me over email. 
 Beijing seems to be paying attention. The day Tencent responded to the incident, the government released proposed export controls covering advanced AI, including agents that can autonomously plan and coordinate. The rules are broader than safety concerns, but the official explanation cites the risk of AI escaping human control. 
 Howard-Jones, meanwhile, called for more transparency. At minimum, she said, firms could agree on a common set of facts to disclose after incidents, giving researchers better data to work with. After the Hugging Face breach, CEO Clement Delangue shared on X that he wonders what would have happened if his firm hadn’t disclosed the OpenAI agent attacks . In his view, we need “100x more transparency in AI,” Clement wrote. He’s correct. 
 One of AI’s oldest thought experiments is the paper clip maximizer. It roughly involves giving a powerful system the seemingly benign task of making as many paper clips as possible, and it eventually brings about the apocalypse after deciding that humans stand in the way of acquiring more resources. Some assumptions underpinning that scenario have aged poorly. 
 Yet the idea that AI doesn’t need evil intentions—or to develop its own—to cause damage is looking increasingly prescient. Agents can create trouble simply by pursuing an ordinary goal long past the point when common sense would stop a human. Still, from San Francisco to Shenzhen, we’re giving these systems more autonomy by the day. ©Bloomberg 
 The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech.

docs.title: Special intensive revision: What's the road ahead for the Election Commission of India?
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Special intensive revision: What's the road ahead for the Election Commission of India?
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 26 Oct 2026, 07:31 AM IST 
 Summary
 The special revision of electoral rolls has seen several issues that left voters out of the draft rolls and raises questions about the process. Here's why India needs more transparency from the Election Commission. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 During the British Raj, only the wealthy and the educated enjoyed the right to vote. After India won freedom, one of the first tasks of the leadership was to expand the electoral rolls to include all eligible adults. This was a formidable task as Partition refugees were still streaming into the country, princely states were yet to be integrated, and the rules of citizenship weren’t finalized by the constituent assembly. 
 Despite stiff odds, independent India’s first draft electoral roll was ready even before the Constitution had been enacted. A small team of civil servants ensured that even the most marginalized inhabitants found a place in the list of voters. 
 When Bengali refugees from what was East Pakistan then complained that they did not have any documents required, the rules were relaxed for them, historian Ornit Shani wrote in How India Became Democratic . The inclusive and empathetic nature of India’s electoral processes , uncommon in the world then, ensured its legitimacy, Shani noted. 
 In contrast, the exclusionary nature of the latest Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has caused a legitimacy crisis for the election commission today. 
 This revision may have begun with the right intentions. An accurate up-to-date list of voters can help check electoral malpractices and make elections representative. 
 But in their zeal to eliminate wrong entries, election officials seem to have gone overboard, denying many voters the right to vote. In West Bengal, many voters found their way back to the voter list only after the elections were over, and after months of bureaucratic paperwork. The process became a test of how badly a citizen wanted to keep her right to vote. 
 It doesn’t take much to imagine the choice an economically weak citizen would make if made to pick between earning daily wages and getting back on the electoral rolls. 
 Not just opposition leaders, some of the government’s most vocal supporters—including a former economic advisor to the prime minister—have raised complaints about being left out of the draft rolls. In Congress-ruled Karnataka, members of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) staged protests against the Commission. 
 After The Indian Express reported that two of the three election commissioners had raised objections about the SIR process, the commission relaxed some of its rules. A 26 September press note said that the updated rules were approved by “the full Commission.” It did not state whether all the SIR rules and changes in voter registration forms had been approved by the full Commission or not. 
 There is no evidence to suggest that the exclusion of legitimate voters favoured the BJP in the Bihar and Bengal elections. But that in itself does not diminish the shortcomings in the process. It was poor and women voters who faced the brunt, since they lacked documents to satisfy an intransigent bureaucracy. 
 India’s political class must strive to re-establish the legitimacy of one of India’s most storied institutions. Rules of appointments to the commission and the manner in which it functions today need to change. 
 The 2023 law that tilted powers towards the government of the day to select election commissioners needs to be revisited. The commission must be independent, and seen to be so. The government needs to reach out to the Opposition and frame a national consensus. The long lever of nation building rests on a fulcrum called negotiation.

docs.title: How the seizure of a Russian vessel brought the Ukraine war to the Arctic
docs.text:
Global 
 How the seizure of a Russian vessel brought the Ukraine war to the Arctic
 Matthew Luxmoore , The Wall Street Journal 7 min read 26 Oct 2026, 06:37 AM IST 
 Summary
 A 12-year legal campaign resulted in Norway’s seizing a research ship in Svalbard, deep in the Arctic Circle. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 SVALBARD, Norway—This summer, Russia’s Geographical Society leased an ice-strengthened vessel for an expedition to map Russia’s historic presence on Norway’s Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
 The sun shone and the waters were calm, the passengers on the Professor Molchanov recalled. What they didn’t know was that Norwegian police would board it at its first stop, the Russian-run mining town of Barentsburg, with a court order to seize the ship and its paperwork.
 The Russians were in no mood to cooperate.
 The episode last month in the High North, just 800 miles from the North Pole, was the latest in a globe-spanning effort to pursue Russian assets that accelerated after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four years ago. Superyachts and private jets of sanctioned Russian oligarchs have been impounded, commercial vessels have been seized, and $300 billion of Russian central-bank assets have been frozen by the European Union.
 The Professor Molchanov, named for a famed Russian scientist, had become a target, too—this time to punish Moscow for one of the first shots in the continuing conflict: its annexation of Crimea in 2014.
 Ukraine’s state energy giant NJSC Naftogaz took legal action to secure compensation from Russia’s Gazprom for energy assets it took over when Russia seized the crucial peninsula on the Black Sea.
 Working with the U.S. law firm Covington & Burling LLP, Naftogaz battled in the courts for nearly a decade with no result. Russia dismissed the case as bogus.
 It wasn’t until April 2023 that an international arbitration tribunal in The Hague ruled that Gazprom had unlawfully expropriated Naftogaz’s Crimean assets. It set compensation at $4.2 billion plus interest, which at the time of the award pushed the total above $5 billion.
 It was a major victory for Ukraine. But Russia refused to pay.
 So began Naftogaz’s secret global search for Russian assets that could be seized to cover its claim, with help from Covington and multiple law firms in other countries.
 Some targets were relatively straightforward. By this fall, Naftogaz had secured the seizure of $500 million worth of Russian-owned real estate in Finland and Austria, according to a list shared with The Wall Street Journal by Covington.
 The operation also zeroed in on assets in Norway. Svalbard, the Norwegian-held territory in the Arctic, was a particular target.
 Russia has long maintained a presence on the archipelago, which became sovereign Norwegian territory a century ago but is governed by a treaty that allows almost any country to do business there.
 The war in Ukraine complicated that arrangement. When Norway joined Western sanctions against Moscow, it stopped issuing visas to most Russians wanting to visit Svalbard. Flying through Oslo or Tromso was no longer an option.
 The Professor Molchanov, a ship that had been traversing Arctic waters on scientific expeditions for more than four decades, offered a workaround. When it resumed voyages to Svalbard in June last year after a long hiatus, it enabled direct passage from Murmansk in Russia’s High North.
 It also caught the attention of Olga Ivaniv, a Ukrainian lawyer at Oslo-based law firm Wikborg Rein, which has worked on Naftogaz’s case at The Hague. Working out of the firm’s London office, she was browsing online one day when she came across the research vessel.
 She learned about its regular trips to Barentsburg, often with tourists on board, and found an itinerary for a voyage slated for late August. Wikborg’s lawyers concluded that the ship wasn’t protected by state immunity laws. They had identified their target.
 The Professor Molchanov set off from Murmansk on Aug. 28. The ship, spanning the width of a soccer pitch, was equipped with two bars, a library and a sauna. Four daily meals included cutlets and mashed potatoes, according to a Russian newspaper reporter on the voyage. Photos of seals decorated the walls of the dining hall.
 The same day a senior partner at Wikborg put in a call to the office of the Svalbard governor—the top law-enforcement official on the Arctic archipelago.
 The partner, Herman Steen, is a shipping expert with almost 25 years of experience. He had already alerted a Norwegian court with jurisdiction over Svalbard that Wikborg would file an urgent request to authorize the ship’s seizure. He now had a message for the Svalbard governor, Lars Fause: prepare to act.
 The news caught Fause by surprise. He had sought to keep good relations with Barentsburg, visiting the town each month to meet with residents and directors of the Russian state-owned mining company that runs it, Arktikugol.
 “It was a big deal,” Fause said in an interview. “You can never be sure about what the Russians are thinking or will do next.”
 Fause decided against immediately carrying out the seizure. When the ship docked in Barentsburg on Sept. 1, his team boarded to conduct a routine border-control procedure.
 When Fause’s team returned the following day to serve a warrant to seize the ship, the Russian captain Sergei Khokhlov was joined by representatives of Arktikugol who refused to hand over the ship’s documents, according to an arrest report shared with the Journal.
 Ildar Neverov, the head of Arktikugol, was out of town but asked to speak by phone with one of the Norwegian police officers. According to the report and lawyers involved in the case, he suggested a misunderstanding had occurred and asked the officer to withdraw. He then warned that seizing the ship would lead to serious consequences, according to the report and lawyers

docs.title: The AI trade is shifting from chip stocks to cybersecurity
docs.text:
Global 
 The AI trade is shifting from chip stocks to cybersecurity
 Paul R. La Monica , Barrons 2 min read 25 Oct 2026, 07:22 AM IST 
 Summary
 Software leaders got a big boost this week and chip stocks were crushed as the AI tech investing landscape continues to shift. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 So much for the so-called SaaSpocalypse.
 Shares of large software -as-a-service companies, such as cybersecurity firms CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks—a Barron’s stock pick in June—were among the top-performing stocks in the S&P 500 this week, with each surging more than 10% during a volatile couple of days for the tech sector and broader market. Elsewhere in the software sector, ServiceNow and Workday each also rose more than 10%.
 Meanwhile, chip stocks got crushed. Semiconductor equipment company Lam Research plunged 13% this week after warning of supply constraints. It’s another sign that the landscape for winners and losers in the artificial-intelligence trade is constantly shifting. Several other semiconductor companies , including Lam rival KLA and AI chip and infrastructure firms Cerebras Systems and Credo Technology, all fell more than 10%.
 Meanwhile, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector exchange-traded fund and the First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF rose 6% and 7% this week, respectively, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 3%. (The broader market ended the week mixed , with the Dow notching a 0.4% gain and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq marking respective losses of 0.5% and 0.7%.)
 Investors, at least for now, seem to be gravitating toward companies that are expected to get a big boost in demand thanks to AI. Think cybersecurity as worries about data breaches and other concerns about rogue AI agents mount. Enterprise software firms are rebounding following a slide earlier this year due to fears—that now appear to have been overblown—about how AI could make big corporate software firms obsolete.
 Meanwhile, there are growing concerns among investors that the rally in chip stocks and other hardware companies—which have been viewed as the biggest beneficiary of hyperscalers such as Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet investing heavily in AI—needs to cool off a bit.
 Along those lines, shares of hard drive maker Western Digital fell Friday despite reporting solid earnings . The stock is up nearly 100% this year.
 Investors should get more clarity about how this dynamic in the tech stock trade is unfolding in the coming week. Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet are all due to report quarterly earnings. So are ServiceNow, cybersecurity firm Fortinet, KLA, Western Digital competitor Seagate, plus Intel and Sandisk.
 Sandisk, for example, is expected to report a year-over-year sales increase of more than 360% and an earnings per share surge of nearly 3,700% from a year ago. Those are not misprints. Demand is booming for Sandisk’s flash memory drives due to AI.
 Could this growth be enough to satisfy investors? Sandisk shares are up more than 420% this year, and the stock is the second-best performer in the S&P 500. But shares fell nearly 5% last week and have plunged more than 30% in the past month.
 As earnings season continues, great results may not be enough to shift the scales back towards AI hardware stocks.

docs.title: Home Loan: Can improving your credit score help you secure a lower interest rate? Experts explain
docs.text:
This is because even a negligible difference in interest rates can meaningfully affect the total interest a borrower pays over the entire repayment period. Now, it is a given that lending institutions consider several factors when determining eligibility and pricing loan offers for home loan applicants; a borrower’s credit score and overall credit profile are also important factors that play a profound role in determining the terms offered. 
 When an individual applicant demonstrates a strong credit profile, it signals responsible borrowing and on-time repayments. Such behaviour can help applicants secure more favourable interest rates. 
 Still, it is equally important to note that improving a credit score does not necessarily guarantee or automatically assure a cheaper home loan, as lending institutions also analyse and check income, existing liabilities, repayment capacity and their own lending policies. 
 Ajai Kumar Shukla, Managing Director & CEO, PNB Housing Finance, explained this aspect in detail, stating, “A strong credit profile can make a tangible difference to the cost of homeownership, especially as interest rates move up. A credit score in the range of 750–900 signals a consistent repayment record, builds lender confidence and can help borrowers qualify for more favourable home loan rates. At the same time, lenders are increasingly leveraging technology and AI-driven credit assessment models to expand access to credit for new-to-credit borrowers or those with limited formal credit histories, including informal income profiles. 
 He further added, "Flexible repayment structures and data-led lending approaches are also helping address diverse borrower needs and make home financing more accessible. It is advisable for Homebuyers to review their credit health report well before applying for a housing loan , as timely repayments and prudent borrowing can strengthen their financial profile for the future." 
 Hence, it is clear that a higher credit score is meaningful, as it can help improve a borrower’s negotiating position; however, the final rate depends on the lending institution’s assessment, deeper analysis, hard checks on the borrower’s profile, and other loan-clearing criteria. Well-informed home loan applicants should, hence, compare offers from multiple lending institutions instead of relying solely on their individual credit scores. 
Atul Monga, CEO and Co-founder of BASIC Home Loan, touched upon this point in detail, explaining, "A healthy credit score plays an important role in determining a borrower's eligibility for a home loan and the interest rate offered by the lender. Borrowers with a low credit score may face loan rejection or be offered a loan at a higher interest rate, while those with a strong credit profile are better positioned to negotiate favourable terms." 
 He further added, "To improve their credit score, borrowers should pay their EMIs and credit card bills on time, reduce outstanding debt and maintain a credit utilisation ratio below 30%. While improving a credit score does not guarantee a lower interest rate, it can strengthen a borrower's negotiating position and improve their chances of securing better home-loan terms." 
 Therefore, it is prudent for aspiring homebuyers to check their credit report for mistakes, errors and omissions, avoid unnecessary loan applications and focus on maintaining a fairly manageable debt level. These steps can help boost and strengthen an individual’s financial profile before applying for a new home loan. 
 In summary, having a high credit score or working to improve a weaker one can both help an individual access better home loan terms. Still, it is only one part of the lending process and decision-making. 
 Maintaining a consistent repayment record, ensuring there are no missed payments or defaults on earlier loans, demonstrating adequate income, and comparing lending institutions carefully, and seeking professional guidance in case of doubts are simple yet effective ways to help aspiring borrowers make a more meaningful and potentially cost-effective home financing decision. 
 Disclaimer: This article is for general information only. Home loan eligibility and interest rates are subject to the lender's policies and individual borrower assessment.

 US manufacturing is adding jobs again, but the hiring rules have changed
 Konrad Putzier , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 26 Oct 2026, 06:53 AM IST 
 Summary
 While factory employment is on the rise, a shift toward high-tech automation is creating roles with greater barriers to entry. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The U.S. is adding manufacturing jobs again. The catch: You might need a college degree to get one.
 That shift has big ramifications for the U.S. economy. Higher-skill jobs tend to pay better and create greater profits for their employers, boosting growth. But because these roles require more education, companies risk a skilled-worker shortage if training programs don’t keep pace.
 Swift Coat, a maker of antireflective coated glass for satellites, plans to hire two or three workers by the end of the year at its facility in a dusty industrial park in northern Phoenix. All positions will require an engineering degree.
 Swift is part of a broader shift in America’s factory landscape. U.S. manufacturers have increased their head count by 72,000 since December, a flicker of hope after years of declining employment. But these aren’t your grandfather’s factory jobs. Manufacturers are hiring more white-collar workers in management and business operations. And blue-collar roles increasingly require advanced training as factories become more automated and complex.
 “The kind of manufacturing that is returning back to the U.S. is not the same as what we used to have in the ’70s or ’80s or ’90s,” said Binil Starly, director of Arizona State University’s School of Manufacturing Systems and Networks. “You need this new worker that is very technology-centric.”
 Between 2015 and 2025, U.S. manufacturers shed 244,000 jobs in so-called production occupations like assemblers and machine operators, according to Labor Department data. Over the same period, they added 358,000 jobs in management and business and financial operations. One factor driving the change is automation: Robots have replaced many shop-floor workers, but not managers and engineers, increasing their share of the workforce.
 Automation has also made factory work more complicated. As companies rely more on sensors and data to track machines and spot potential problems, they need analysts to sift through the numbers. Robots require skilled technicians who can maintain them.
 “Any factory you walk into right now, you just cannot function without at least an understanding of how these systems are operational,” ASU’s Starly said.
 Phoenix-based Swift uses highly complex machinery to turn tiny particles called nanomaterials into antireflective coating, which can help make satellite-powered solar panels more effective, among other applications.
 The startup’s seven-person full-time staff includes a physics Ph.D., two people with a master’s in mechanical engineering and one with a bachelor’s in chemical engineering, CEO Peter Firth said. They do work like running computer simulations, analyzing data, designing equipment and testing the coating. Of the three shop-floor technicians who handle and inspect samples, one has an associate degree, and another spent some time in college. They are also experienced.
 “If everything is working perfectly, I could pull my mom in and she could do the work,” Firth said. “But we hire people in those roles to prevent and to identify problems. So you really want someone that has the right type of experience to be able to do that effectively.”
 Swift is investing in a new assembly line that will be highly automated—robots load and unload samples, while one or two workers keep a watchful eye. That means that instead of hiring five technicians, the company might hire one technician and two engineers, who will be paid more, according to Firth. “We’re not necessarily spending less on people,” he said.
 While older industries such as furniture making are shrinking, knowledge-intensive industries like aerospace, computers, electrical equipment and heating and cooling systems have been adding workers this year. In airplane manufacturing, more than half of workers have at least a bachelor’s degree, according to the Census Bureau. Meanwhile, semiconductor makers are more likely to hire college graduates than other manufacturers, according to a LinkedIn analysis.
 These higher-skill jobs not only pay better, they often involve less “drudgery and mind-numbing tasks” than the assembly-line work of past decades, said Susan Houseman, an economist at the W.E. Upjohn Institute of Employment Research.
 On the flip side, higher training requirements mean bigger barriers to entry. The days when people could walk out of high school and straight into a factory are increasingly over. “What I worry about is the access to good jobs,” said Susan Helper, an economist at Case Western Reserve University’s Weatherhead School of Management.
 Companies and industry groups, worried about a skilled-worker shortage, are racing to expand training. The manufacturing trade group SME employs around 125 people in its workforce development division and sends equipment such as drone-coding kits and 3-D printers to middle schools in an effort to get kids excited about factory work. “Technology is now outpacing our people,” said CEO Jeannine Kunz. “There’s not a manufacturing sector that’s not starving for talent.”
 In Mesa, Arizona, ASU’s school of manufacturing is training around 170 people to become equipment technicians at Taiwanese chip maker TSMC’s fast-growing Arizona plant and plans to increase that number to 800 next year. The school, which was founded five years ago, also has around 370 students studying for bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees.

docs.title: The earnings boom is heavily reliant on just a handful of stocks
docs.text:
Global 
 The earnings boom is heavily reliant on just a handful of stocks
 Hannah Erin Lang , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 25 Oct 2026, 07:15 AM IST 
 Summary
 Ten companies—including Nvidia, Micron and other AI giants—account for roughly two-thirds of corporate profit growth. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Wall Street has rested much of its optimism about the stock market on a surge in corporate earnings. The catch is that the profit growth is being driven by a handful of AI giants.
 Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to report a 30% jump in third-quarter earnings from a year ago, according to FactSet, boosting investor confidence that the good times can keep rolling so long as businesses keep printing money. But just two companies—Nvidia and Micron—account for 34% of that growth, according to a Dow Jones Market Data analysis.
 And only 10 companies—including Broadcom and Meta Platforms—account for roughly two-thirds of the profit growth. Others include oil-and-gas giants that benefited from higher energy prices caused by the conflict in Iran.
 It is another way the U.S. stock market has come to depend on a handful of companies tied to the artificial-intelligence trade—and the fervid race to build the infrastructure that supports the technology, as costly as it may become.
 The risk posed by that concentrated earnings growth, analysts said, is the same one underpinning the broader AI investing boom: that the technology ultimately won’t deliver on the massive sums of money being poured into it.
 In other words, the fear is that “we’re going to end up converting all these data centers into pickleball facilities,” said longtime stock analyst Ed Yardeni.
 Those worries resurfaced this past week, when Meta’s plans for a cash-raising spree helped trigger one of the Nasdaq’s worst selloffs this year.
 Many investors aren’t too concerned with extraordinary profit growth being driven by a small group of companies. For one, earnings across the market are still growing, albeit at a slower pace. Even without the top 10 stocks juicing growth, the rest of the S&P 500 is expected to deliver a 10% jump in profit from a year ago—a respectable showing, especially for a bull market that has now stretched into its fourth year, said Chris Grisanti, chief market strategist at MAI Capital Management.
 The companies with the fastest growth are “the best on an all-star team right now,” he said, “but the rest of the team is carrying its weight.”
 Another reason to be optimistic: investors are already factoring in that the supersize profit increases won’t last forever.
 Even as earnings estimates surged this year, share prices—for the market and the firms driving the growth—have moved relatively little in comparison. That means equities look cheaper than they did at the start of the year.
 “The market is being uncharacteristically wise,” Grisanti said. “We’re not in anything like euphoria.”
 Still, Grisanti said his team is among those preparing for an earnings slowdown, shifting from “picks and shovels” plays to take a larger position in power providers. As the data-center build-out progresses, the thinking is that demand for electricity will keep growing even as memory-chip supply constraints ease.
 For Nvidia and Micron, profits have been fueled by extraordinary demand for memory and other AI chips that has given suppliers extraordinary pricing power. The numbers are eye-popping: last month, Micron reported that its quarterly profit had multiplied more than 10-fold from the year prior, or 1,078%. Analysts expect a 90% leap for Nvidia, according to FactSet.
 Money managers have for months pointed to climbing corporate profits as a crucial reason why stocks could blow past a list of anxieties that included rising interest rates, conflict in the Middle East and a bond market set on edge .
 But the momentum in artificial-intelligence stocks isn’t just about the profits companies are generating now, it is also about the projection that mammoth demand for AI tools will translate into big profits well into the future. Whenever that excitement dims even a little bit—over concerns about availability of capital or completion of data centers—investors pull back.
 Analysts said it is likely those doubts will keep surfacing periodically on Wall Street, with this past week serving as an example. The cycle has earned many comparisons with the dot-com boom of the late ‘90s, another tech-driven bull market with a famously unhappy ending.
 Larry Adam, chief investment officer at Raymond James, thinks there is one key difference with the comparison: dot-com companies weren’t making money like this.
 “This is not back to 2000,” he said. “In many ways, I think the market has been pretty rational.”
