News 
 Eternal’s District explores live-event venues to cut concert costs, counter AI threat
 Sowmya Ramasubramanian 4 min read 26 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 The out-of-home consumption platform is exploring partnerships with property owners and governments to build dedicated venues as it seeks to scale its events business and strengthen its defences against AI-led disruption. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 BENGALURU: Eternal’s District is exploring investments in dedicated live-event venues, betting that physical infrastructure can lower the cost of staging concerts and give the out-of-home consumption platform a more defensible business as artificial intelligence (AI) agents threaten to disrupt online bookings.
 The company is in discussions with potential partners and governments on long-term projects, including public-private partnerships, Rahul Ganjoo, chief executive of District, said in an interview with Mint .
 “Without dedicated live-event venues, it is difficult to build a sustainable business, because you spend a large amount of money setting up a venue only to take it down within a day,” Ganjoo said. Some temporary concert sites can cost over $1 million to build only to be dismantled within hours, he added.
 District’s first bet is Terraform, a 16-acre outdoor entertainment arena in north Bengaluru, which it took over in September 2025. Its plug-and-play model includes facilities for artists, production crews, and audiences, reducing the need to build infrastructure from scratch for each concert.
 Building new venues, however, will take time. Large additions to the network are unlikely within the next year, Ganjoo said. “It will be a long-drawn-out process. In the meantime, we’re exploring opportunities and working with partners to identify potential venues,” he added.
 Supply constraints 
 District plans to focus initially on five to 10 major cities, where event supply and audience demand can support regular programming. It is also engaging with stakeholders in 10 to 15 cities to assess commercial viability.
 Mumbai remains a particularly competitive market for concert infrastructure, Ganjoo said. The company is also exploring smaller venues for recurring events, allowing performers and formats to build audiences before moving to larger stages. Ganjoo declined to share specifics.
 The strategy reflects a broader push to cater to consumers seeking more varied leisure experiences, from nostalgia-led concerts to weekday outings. “The overarching theme is that people want to spend more on different experiences, and not the same thing, to break that monotony,” Ganjoo said.
 But building a venue network is only part of the challenge. Ankur Bisen, senior partner at retail consultancy The Knowledge Company, said District must first define the proposition it wants to offer, weighing options such as buying venues, building them or partnering with property owners.
 “You have to rebuild this category from scratch,” Bisen said, citing considerations such as accessibility, urban planning and public safety.
 He cautioned against assuming that expansion would require heavy investment in property. “It does not require heavy investment in real estate to make venues work. You can always hire out or operate a plug-and-play,” he said. Underutilized malls and other properties could provide space for operators with successful event concepts, Bisen added.
 Ultimately, the proposition matters as much as the property itself. “You are limited by your own imagination in this space,” Bisen said.
 AI threat 
 The venue strategy comes as Eternal flags the potential disruption of District’s business by AI agents, which could allow consumers to discover and book experiences without relying on the platform.
 In its shareholder letter for the second quarter of fiscal year 2027 (Q2FY27), Eternal placed District in the “medium-to-high risk zone” for agent-led commerce. Unlike food delivery and quick commerce, where fulfilment infrastructure is central to the service, some of District’s offerings, including restaurant reservations and non-exclusive concert tickets, exist independently of the platform and can be accessed through other channels.
 Eternal said the risk has made physical infrastructure and differentiated customer experiences important to District’s long-term prospects.
 “A large part of durability in this business will come from building physical infrastructure and operations which deliver a differentiated customer experience,” Eternal’s chief financial officer Akshant Goyal said in the letter. “Like we mentioned earlier, where infrastructure becomes the product.”
 The strategy will need to deliver growth while improving the platform’s financial performance. In the September quarter of FY27, District recorded net order value (NOV) of ₹ 3,259 crore, up 58% from a year earlier and 1.3% sequentially. NOV is the gross value of all orders minus discounts.
 Its adjusted Ebitda loss was ₹ 64 crore, while its adjusted Ebitda margin improved to -2% of NOV from -3.1% a year earlier.
 Eternal said District remained on track to reach adjusted Ebitda break-even within four to six quarters. It has set FY30 targets of ₹ 28,000 crore in NOV and ₹ 1,400 crore in adjusted Ebitda.
 Beyond live events, District is also looking to make discovery and planning across leisure categories more seamless. Travel is among the categories consumers frequently ask about, but the company has yet to establish a clear strategy for entering it, Ganjoo said.

Explainer Mint Explainer | Is India’s tech workforce AI-ready? Samiksha Goel 3 min read 25 Oct 2026, 04:42 PM IST Summary India faces a widening gap between demand for AI skills and the supply of job-ready professionals, reshaping hiring, salaries and career prospects across the technology industry. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now As companies move artificial intelligence (AI) from experimentation to business operations, demand for specialized skills is outstripping supply. India faces a demand-supply gap of more than 3.5 times, according to recent talent intelligence from BinQle. The shortage is reshaping pay, too. TeamLease Digital’s Digital Skills and Salary Primer 2026-27 , based on an analysis of 37,000 technology and digital roles, finds that compensation increasingly reflects the depth of a professional’s AI capabilities rather than job title, tenure or location. Mint examines where the shortages are most acute, how AI is changing job profiles and salaries, and what this means for the technology industry. Where is the gap most acute? The shortage spans both the number of professionals available and the specific skills employers need. BinQle estimates that India will need 1.4 million AI professionals by 2026, against an available pool of 400,000. It also flags shortages in adjacent technology roles, including data engineering, cloud architecture and DevOps. The TeamLease report identifies cloud as having the widest supply gap among four high-value skills—AI, data, cloud and cybersecurity—at 55-60%. Generative AI follows at about 53%, with demand for GenAI talent expected to exceed 1 million roles by 2026. The gap in cybersecurity stands at 25-30%, narrowing but still significant. Why can’t universities fill the gap? Universities are producing technology graduates, but degrees do not necessarily translate into job-ready skills. TeamLease Digital’s report points to growing employer demand for specialized capabilities, including building AI systems, integrating them into business workflows and managing the underlying infrastructure. Traditional curricula can struggle to keep pace with rapidly evolving technologies and may not provide enough exposure to real-world deployment. Revising courses and developing practical, industry-relevant training takes time, leaving companies to play a larger role in preparing workers through specialised programmes and reskilling. Which sectors are seeing the greatest disruption? AI adoption is most visible in financial services, retail, IT, healthcare and logistics, although its applications vary by sector. Financial services companies use AI to detect fraud, assess risk and automate customer interactions. Retailers apply it to demand forecasting, inventory planning, pricing and personalized marketing. In IT services, generative AI is automating parts of software development, testing and customer support, putting pressure on traditional delivery models. Healthcare applications include medical imaging, clinical decision support and patient management. Logistics companies use AI to optimize routes, forecast demand and manage warehouses. Are salaries rising, too? The shortage of specialized, job-ready professionals is putting upward pressure on pay, though gains vary by role. BinQle reports salary increases of 30-35% in specialized technology roles. TeamLease Digital’s analysis suggests that pay increasingly depends on the depth of AI expertise. Entry-level AI-Core roles, including generative AI and machine-learning engineering, command 2.5-3 times the pay of AI-Support roles. TeamLease projects salary growth of 16-21% for AI-Core positions between fiscal year 2027 (FY27) and FY28, against 7-8% for AI-Support roles. Senior professionals who combine technical expertise with architecture, governance, security or domain knowledge can command higher premiums. What does this mean for the tech industry? The talent crunch could reshape how technology companies hire , train and deploy workers. Employers may need to compete more aggressively for experienced professionals while investing in reskilling rather than relying solely on external recruitment. The divide could also widen between workers who build and deploy AI systems and those who support AI-enabled operations, affecting career progression and pay. Over time, the shortage may push companies and educational institutions to rethink how technology skills are taught and assessed, as traditional qualifications alone become a less reliable measure of workplace readiness. Opinion 
 How China’s industrial strength is testing its growth model
 G. Venkat Raman 3 min read 26 Oct 2026, 12:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 The country's industrial competitiveness has not translated into equally strong domestic demand, while its export competitiveness is provoking resistance from overseas markets like the European Union. How Beijing manages these competing priorities will matter beyond China. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 China’s economic recovery remains fragile despite its industrial strength, Reuters reported on 20 October, citing an official from the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), China’s top economic planning agency.
 The warning followed a 36.3% year-on-year surge in September exports, driven partly by semiconductors, automobiles and other technology products. Yet, domestic consumption is subdued and resistance to Chinese exports is growing.
 With the Fifth Plenum of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee having commenced, Beijing faces a difficult question: can it sustain industrial expansion without stronger domestic demand?
 Official figures released last week revealed the extent of this divergence. China’s economy grew 4.5% year-on-year in the third quarter, while industrial output increased 5.5% in September. But retail sales rose just 1.1%, and fixed-asset investment declined 7.2% during the first nine months. These show an imbalance between industrial resilience and domestic demand.
 These weaknesses, however, should not obscure the foundations of China’s industrial competitiveness, which extend beyond state subsidies. In electric vehicles and batteries, sustained investment, integrated supplier networks and economies of scale have enabled manufacturers to compete on technology and price.
 In AI, domestic firms are innovating despite restrictions on advanced semiconductors, although dependence on foreign chips persists. These achievements reflect state coordination, private entrepreneurship, domestic competition and accumulated manufacturing expertise.
 Yet, industrial competitiveness has not translated into equally strong domestic demand. The NDRC has described this imbalance as gong qiang xu ruo (strong supply, weak demand). Industrial upgradation has yet to generate broad income and employment gains capable of sustaining household consumption.
 The 15th Five-Year Plan seeks to strengthen consumption alongside technological self-reliance and xin zhi shengchanli (new quality productive forces). The challenge is to reconcile stronger household demand with Beijing’s emphasis on industrial and technological expansion.
 China’s prolonged property downturn has weakened household confidence, while employment uncertainty and precautionary savings are restraining consumption even as incomes rise. Local governments, central to infrastructure and industrial investment, face fiscal pressures from declining land revenues and accumulated debt. Greater political centralization may also discourage local officials from exercising discretion.
 Competition to attract industries helped build manufacturing clusters but encouraged duplicative investment and price wars that hurt profitability. Beijing’s criticism of neijuan shi jingzheng (involution-style competition) reflects concern that growing production does not necessarily generate corresponding profits or productivity gains.
 The challenge is to raise investment efficiency without undermining the competition that built China’s industrial strength.
 These tensions extend beyond China’s domestic economy. With demand subdued, overseas markets are a vital outlet for Chinese manufacturers. Yet, their export competitiveness is provoking resistance.
 This month, the European Union (EU) and China reached a preliminary understanding to curb Chinese hybrid-car exports, while France and Germany pressed for stronger EU trade-defence measures. Such restrictions could accelerate Chinese manufacturers’ shift towards production within Europe.
 These external pressures make strengthening local demand more urgent. In July, China’s State Council approved a five-year consumption plan covering household incomes, social security and services. Earlier this month, NDRC chairman Zheng Shanjie signalled further policy support. Yet, stronger consumption depends not only on government steps but also household confidence, income expectations and social protection.
 The Fifth Plenum’s focus on party governance is relevant to implementing these economic measures. At its July meeting, the Politburo discussed the Plenum’s agenda alongside calls to expand domestic demand, curb involution-style competition and improve conditions for private enterprise.
 In August, Xi Jinping called for better evaluation of officials, following a campaign against wasteful projects and superficial achievements. How officials are assessed influences investment decisions and policy implementation. The test is whether tighter Party supervision can improve economic decision-making while allowing selective decentralization that preserves local initiative and encourages private investment.
 How Beijing manages these competing priorities will matter beyond China. Stronger domestic consumption could reduce reliance on exports, while persistent imbalances may intensify international price competition. American technology firms face China’s continuing innovation despite restrictions, while European manufacturers confront formidable Chinese rivals.
 Indian businesses benefit from affordable Chinese machinery and components even as competing imports pressure domestic manufacturers. Supply-chain diversification may change where goods are assembled without eliminating dependence on Chinese inputs.
 The Fifth Plenum will not resolve China’s economic contradictions, but it will test whether tighter party governance can improve decision-making.

 Travel: On a lemon trail along Italy’s Amalfi Coast
 Teja Lele 5 min read 25 Oct 2026, 10:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 The Sentiero dei Limoni, which winds through centuries-old villages, reveals the coast’s deep-rooted relationship with its most iconic fruit 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Lemons are everywhere on the Amalfi Coast: in market stalls, on ceramics, flavouring everything from pasta to pastries, and in countless glasses of limoncello. But to understand the role these bright, fragrant fruits play in the region, one must leave the coastal road and take a walk.
 The Sentiero dei Limoni, or Path of the Lemons, is an ancient route connecting the coastal towns of Maiori and Minori. The path, roughly 2.5 miles, climbs through terraced lemon groves, narrow alleys and small settlements, with stunning views of the Gulf of Salerno. It takes about an hour to 90 minutes, longer if you stop for the views.
 For centuries, Sentiero dei Limoni was a working route, connecting villages, agricultural terraces and the sea.
 “Lemon cultivation has played a fundamental role in shaping both the landscape and the economy of the Amalfi Coast,” explains Fra Marcus, a Franciscan friar and cultural guide at Anantara Convento di Amalfi Grand Hotel. “As the terrain is extremely steep, local communities created terraces supported by dry-stone walls, transforming inaccessible slopes into productive agricultural land.”
 A STEP BACK IN TIME
 The walk begins in Maiori, near the 13th-century Collegiata di Santa Maria a Mare, a church overlooking the town. Stone steps lead uphill along Via Vena, past old walls that once protected the lemon groves. There are about 400 steps along the route, so comfortable shoes and water are a must.
 As the town recedes, lemon trees come into view beneath pergolas supported by chestnut poles. Beyond the terraces grow olive trees, vines, and carob trees, locally called sciuscelle. Chapels, gardens, and stone walls line the route, alongside the sea.
 The path passes through the hamlet of Torre and its church of San Michele Arcangelo, located midway between Maiori and Minori. The quiet lanes, old houses, and working farms hark back to the coast’s agricultural past.
 “Before the construction of the coastal road, routes such as the Sentiero dei Limoni were essential connections between settlements, cultivated terraces and the sea,” Marcus says. “The path linked Maiori and Minori through San Michele and the ancient village of Torre, allowing residents to move between the two towns and reach the lemon groves above them.”
 Lemons became particularly valuable because their vitamin C helped protect sailors against scurvy. As early as the 11th century, the Maritime Republic of Amalfi required ships to carry citrus supplies. Between the 15th and 19th centuries, demand for Amalfi lemons grew, particularly in northern Europe.
 CHANGING TIMES
 The fruit at the centre of it all is the Sfusato Amalfitano, named for its elongated, spindle-like shape. Larger than ordinary lemons, it has a thick, aromatic rind, relatively few seeds and juicy flesh. Even the white pith is edible.
 Giovanni Romano, who leads walking tours along the path, explains what makes the variety distinctive.
 “The climate in southern Italy, the nutrients in the soil, the dry terracing that gives the plants air, the chestnut-pole pergolas that hold up the heavy branches, the organic fertiliser made from manure, and the plastic netting over the trees in winter create exemplary growing conditions,” he says.
 Harvesting begins in February in gardens closest to the sea and continues until late October in cooler inland groves. Sacks of lemons are often carried downhill by hand. The work is often described as agricoltura eroica, or heroic agriculture.
 In Amalfi, the Aceto family has cultivated lemons for generations, beginning in 1825 when Salvatore Aceto purchased a small plot of land in Ravello. Today, his namesake runs the family business, which offers guided tours of its terraced groves from March to November, along with cooking classes on local lemon dishes.
 The Amalfi Coast’s terraced lemon-growing system was recognised by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System in 2025. Yet ageing farming communities, difficult access, and the abandonment of remote terraces threaten this landscape.
 Francesco Damiano, an environmental hiking guide and filmmaker nicknamed the Neapolitan Indiana Jones, works to raise awareness of this heritage. “My work sheds light on and raises awareness of our forgotten, or worse, ignored, cultural and artistic heritage,” he says.
 Michele Ruocco, a retired banker turned agronomist and member of non-profit Pro Loco Minori, is also working to create awareness. He says the path is best experienced through all five senses. “Listen to the sounds of nature,” he says, referring to the wind, waves, and birdsong. And, the smell. “Smells remain in our minds and convey emotions and memories.”
 A hike up the Path of Lemons offers the chance to taste local produce along the way. Farms offer fresh lemonade, marmalade and traditional lemon salad, made with sliced lemon, olive oil, salt, pepper and mint.
 The Sfusato also appears in seafood dishes, pasta, cakes and pastries. In Amalfi, the Pansa pastry shop on Piazza Duomo, founded in 1830, serves delizia al limone, a dome-shaped sponge cake soaked in limoncello syrup, filled with lemon cream and covered in a lemon glaze. Created in 1978 by Sorrento pastry chef Carmine Marzuillo, it has become one of the region’s best-known desserts. In Minori, pastry chef Sal De Riso continues to use the lemon as a signature ingredient in his creations.

Nifty reverses recent gains amid global headwinds; Cautious outlook prevails The Indian equity markets witnessed a turbulent, truncated trading week, with the Nifty50 index reversing its recent uptrend and surrendering gains accumulated over the previous two weeks. Deteriorating global cues and a sharp surge in crude oil prices weighed heavily on investor sentiment, triggering a corrective phase. The benchmark index remained under sustained selling pressure throughout the week, reflecting heightened caution among market participants. Consequently, the Nifty50 index ended the week at 22,600, registering a substantial decline of 2.36 per cent, thereby weakening the near-term market outlook. The broader market witnessed widespread weakness, with the mid-cap and small-cap indices registering significant declines, further dampening the overall market sentiment. The across-the-board sell-off intensified the ongoing correction, reflecting heightened investor caution and a deterioration in market breadth. From a technical perspective, the Nifty50 index failed to sustain above its 20-DEMA after struggling around for a couple of sessions. The index subsequently extended its decline towards the recent lows. Moreover, the 14-day RSI has delivered a negative crossover, signaling weakening momentum and warranting a cautious approach in the coming week. On the levels, 22,500 remains a crucial juncture, a decisive breach below this level could accelerate the decline towards 22,200 on intermediate basis, with the psychological mark of 22,000 potentially coming into focus thereafter. On the upside, the 20-DEMA, placed around 22,840, is likely to act as an immediate resistance and a sustained move above this hurdle would be essential to revive positive momentum and pave the way for a potential retest of 23,000, followed by 23,150 in the near term. At present, the near-term bias remains tilted towards the downside, although the broader directional trend lacks definitive confirmation. Given the prevailing uncertainty and mixed technical signals, a measured, step-by-step approach would be prudent rather than taking aggressive directional positions. Going forward, market participants should closely monitor the aforementioned technical levels while remaining vigilant about evolving global developments, particularly movements in crude oil prices and broader international market trends. These factors are likely to play a pivotal role in determining the market's near-term trajectory. A cautious and selective strategy appears warranted until the market establishes a more convincing trend. MF investor growth slows further as equities falter, launches decline
 Industry adds 4.4 million new investors in first 9 months of 2026, slowest since covid-hit 2020
 premium 
 Mutual fund investor additions slow to 4.4 million till September as market volatility and fewer new fund launches weigh on growth.
 Abhishek Kumar Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 7:23 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 The mutual fund (MF) investor growth trajectory remains on the slower side for the second consecutive year, coinciding with the weakness in equity market and a slowdown in new fund launches. The industry has added 4.4 million net new investors in calendar year 2026 (CY26) till September. This is the slowest pace of additions since 2023, when the industry had added 3.7 million investors in the first 9 months. 
 The unique MF investor count is the total number of PANs registered with the industry. At the end of September 2026, the total investor count was 63.3 million, shows industry data sourced by Business Standard. 
 The MF investor growth — along with other metrics like folios and assets under management — has traditionally been dependent on the equity market performance. 
 Fund houses had added about 10 million investors in each of 2021 and 2024 when the equity market was witnessing a bull run. In the rest of the years post covid, the additions have been around 5-6 million. 
 Experts said the additions in 2026, while seeming low, is closer to the average pace of growth seen by the industry. 
 “2024 proved exceptional, and it is advisable to treat it as an outlier rather than a standard benchmark. The influx of new investors closely aligns with market sentiment; the robust 2024 rally attracted many first-time and short-term participants. However, since then, market conditions have become more volatile, and regulators have imposed stricter guidelines on higher-risk trading, which has understandably slowed new sign-ups,” said Vipul Bhowar, executive director, head of equities, Waterfield Advisors. 
 Aditya Agarwal, cofounder of Wealthy.in, said the growth is actually on a strong footing considering the volatility and global uncertainties. 
 “Adding 4.4 million new investors in a year of volatile markets, a rate hike and geopolitical uncertainty is a sign of resilience, not weakness. The pace is almost the same as last year. It was 2024 that was the exception, when an unusually strong market brought first-time investors in at a record pace. New investors naturally take their cue from recent returns, and the past two years have been choppier,” said the Cofounder of the wealth management platform for mutual fund distributors. 
 While the market performance is an important metric, investor addition also depends on new fund launches by fund houses. The launches as well as the investor interest for new fund offerings have declined in the past two years. 
 “New fund offering collections fell to a five-year low of about ₹1,759 crore in this year’s April-June quarter, as tighter regulation reduced the thematic launches that historically brought in new PANs. New fund launches were the industry’s most effective acquisition channel, and that channel has quietened,” said Akshat Garg, head-research & product at Choice Wealth.

docs.text: Brokerage consensus stocks: Several Indian stocks have drawn positive recommendations from multiple brokerages following the September-quarter earnings season, with analysts weighing growth prospects against rising costs, competitive pressures and valuations. Swiggy, Eternal, Bajaj Finance, UltraTech Cement, Oberoi Realty and InterGlobe Aviation have attracted 'Buy' calls from at least two brokerage firms, with target prices suggesting varying degrees of potential upside. Top brokerage recommendations 1. Swiggy Motilal Oswal Motilal Oswal has a 'Buy' rating on Swiggy with a target price of Rs 280, implying an upside of 32%. The brokerage's assessment rests on the value of Swiggy's food delivery business and its ability to build a profitable quick-commerce operation through Instamart. The brokerage remains cautious about the pace of improvement in Instamart's economics. Motilal Oswal expects revenue growth to moderate in the second half of FY27 and adjusted EBITDA losses to increase from Rs 1,360 crore to Rs 1,490 crore. Jefferies Jefferies has assigned Swiggy a target price of Rs 330, indicating an upside of 48%. The brokerage found the company's food delivery performance broadly in line with expectations, but quick commerce remained under pressure, with adjusted EBITDA losses reaching around Rs 9 billion, their highest level in three quarters. Its assessment takes account of the difference between Swiggy's operating performance and that of Eternal, particularly in quick-commerce execution. Jefferies believes Swiggy's share price does not fully account for the value of its food delivery business and cash balance. However, it considers a reduction in quick-commerce losses essential before the market can place greater value on the business. Nuvama Nuvama has the highest target price among the Swiggy recommendations listed here, at Rs 403, implying an upside of around 91%. The brokerage reported that Swiggy's revenue increased 11.1% quarter-on-quarter to Rs 7,570 crore in Q2FY27, while EBITDA and net losses widened to Rs 770 crore and Rs 920 crore, respectively. Food delivery contribution margin improved to 7.7%, but Instamart's contribution margin declined to minus 1%. The brokerage expects Instamart's contribution margin to recover in the third quarter, with further improvement possible as the business transitions towards an inventory-led model. 2. Eternal Motilal Oswal Motilal Oswal has a 'Buy' rating on Eternal with a target price of Rs 420, suggesting an upside of around 35%. The brokerage's analysis focuses on the strong growth of Blinkit and the performance of Zomato's food delivery business. Despite the earnings shortfall, Motilal Oswal expects Blinkit's expanding store network and the maturation of existing outlets to support growth. It also expects food delivery to remain a priority, with margins broadly stable over the next one to two years. Jefferies Jefferies has a 'Buy' rating on Eternal and a target price of Rs 430, implying an upside of 38%. Its analysis includes the company's proposed dark.ai artificial intelligence assistant, a privacy-focused product that could create an additional opportunity beyond food delivery and quick commerce. The brokerage acknowledged that questions remain about the product's competitive advantage, investment requirements and ability to generate revenue. However, it has noted that the financial impact of dark.ai is difficult to assess without more details about the product and its commercial prospects. AUM increased 26% year-on-year, net interest income rose 24%, and adjusted profit after tax grew 34%, according to the research summary. docs.title: Radhakishan Damani and Mukul Agrawal’s stock picks: A cash cow and a luxury wedding bet
docs.text: Radhakishan Damani & Mukul Agrawal Portfolio: Fresh Big Moves Revealed Every quarter, portfolio trackers flag a fresh crop of "new buys" by super investors. This time, two of the most watched names in Indian markets show up with new entries. Mukul Agrawal appears in Purple Style Labs with a 1.25% stake. Radhakishan Damani, the founder of DMart, appears in the National Stock Exchange with 1.58%. Look closer, though, and neither is a buy in the usual sense. Both companies listed only in September 2026. So, the September filing is simply the first time these holdings had to be shown to the market. Damani picked up his NSE shares in early 2020. Mukul Agrawal was already a shareholder in Purple Style Labs before its IPO opened in August. That difference matters more than it sounds. Investors who bought these shares at the IPO are sitting on losses. Early backers like Damani and Mukul Agrawal are not selling. One company is among the most profitable businesses in India. The other has not yet made a profit. Here is what each one looks like today. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 National Stock Exchange: Damani's Rs 6,600 Crore Stake in India's Toll Road for Trading Incorporated in November 1992, the National Stock Exchange of India is the country's largest stock exchange. Almost every Nifty trade, option contract and mutual fund order a retail investor places passes through its systems. It earns a small fee on each one. Its IPO was one of the most awaited in Indian market history. The issue ran from 17th to 21st September 2026, priced at Rs 1,785 a share, and raised about Rs 22,563 cr. Every rupee went to selling shareholders such as State Bank of India and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board. NSE itself raised nothing. The issue was subscribed 5.71 times, and the shares listed on BSE on 24th September. NSE cannot list on its own platform. Damani was not among the sellers. He bought his stake from Norwest Venture Partners in early 2020. After a 4:1 bonus issue in 2024, he holds 3.91 crore shares. At the closing price of Rs 1,688 on 22nd October 2026, that stake is worth about Rs 6,600 cr. Within his public portfolio, only his DMart holding is larger. NSE Share Price Target: Why the Stock is Trading Below IPO Issue Price Few listed companies look like this on paper. Financial YearFY22FY23FY24FY25FY264Y CAGRSales (Rs cr)8,31311,85614,78017,14116,60119%EBITDA (Rs cr)6,6059,4299,87312,67111,26514%Net Profit (Rs cr)5,1987,3568,30612,18810,30219% Source: Screener.in EBITDA is operating profit before other income. Screener's consolidated history for NSE begins in FY22, so a four-year CAGR is shown in place of five. Sales have doubled in four years. Operating margin was 68% in FY26, and borrowings are a mere Rs 412 cr. Return on equity has averaged about 35% over three years. The exchange paid out 84% of FY26 profit as dividends. But look at the last column of figures again. FY26 was the first down year in the table. Sales slipped 3% and net profit fell 15%, after SEBI tightened rules on futures and options trading by retail investors. Other income, mostly returns on investments, was Rs 3,417 cr in FY26, about a quarter of profit before tax. The June 2026 quarter showed some steadiness. Net profit rose 7% from a year earlier to Rs 3,120 cr, on sales of Rs 4,560 cr. NSE has also moved to close its long-running co-location and dark fibre cases with SEBI through a settlement of about Rs 1,491 cr, according to its results filing. ALSO READVijay Kedia’s latest bets: Rs 73 cr in 2 smallcaps with surging profits NSE Below IPO Price: What Retail Allottees Are Facing The share price of NSE touched Rs 1,878 on listing day. As of closing on 22nd October 2026, it was Rs 1,688, which is 5% below the issue price and 10% below that high. The stock has been listed for less than a month, so there is no five-year price record to compare. On valuations, NSE trades at a PE of 46x, the same as the current industry median of 46x. A 10-year median PE for the company is not meaningful after one month of trading. The industry median for the same period is 41x. Two pressures are worth watching. One is regulation, because SEBI can reshape derivatives volumes with a single circular. The other is rivalry. BSE's F&O turnover crossed NSE's for the first time in April. Supply is a third, shorter-term factor. Half of the anchor investors' shares became free to sell on 21st October 2026, and the rest unlock on 20th December. NSE reports its September quarter numbers on 3rd November 2026. #2 Purple Style Labs: Mukul Agrawal's Bet on India's Rs 10,000 Crore Luxury Wedding Market Incorporated in August 2015, Purple Style Labs runs Pernia's Pop-Up Shop. It sells Indian designer wear, mostly for weddings and big occasions, through its website, app and large experience centres in Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad, London and New York. Its customers spend big. In India, the average store order is about Rs 90,000. The company's founder, Abhishek Agarwal, estimates that luxury makes up about 5% of India's Rs 2 Lakh Crore wedding and occasion-wear market. Shah Rukh Khan's family trust, Madhuri Dixit and Sachin Tendulkar were among its pre-IPO shareholders. So was Mukul Agrawal. The company's red herring prospectus listed him with 10 lakh shares, or 1.37% of the pre-issue capital. He did not sell, and the fresh shares issued in the IPO diluted him to 1.25%. That stake is worth about Rs 51 cr today. His entry price is not disclosed. For context, the founder sold about Rs 45 cr of his own shares in August 2025 at Rs 500 each. The IPO raised Rs 680 cr at Rs 575 a share, all through fresh shares, and was subscribed just 1.19 times. The stock listed on 7th September 2026. docs.title: Massive Rs 64,000 cr order books: 2 Indian stocks cashing in on AI’s hunger for fibre
docs.text: Artificial intelligence is changing the way data centres are designed. As network speeds move from 400G to 800G and 1.6T, copper cabling is reaching its physical limits. This is driving demand for optical fibre. The need for fibre is also rising within and between server racks. Fibre counts in switch racks have increased from around 500 in conventional cloud setups to 12,000 in 72-GPU server nodes. Future designs could require up to 16,000 fibres per rack, 32X more than the 500 required in conventional setups. For optical fibre manufacturers, this shift is creating an opportunity to move beyond conventional telecom cables and supply specialised products for AI infrastructure. Two companies are already seeing the impact in their financial performance. One reported a 448% year-on-year jump in net profit to ₹394 crore in Q2FY27, while the other recorded net profit of ₹517 crore, compared with just ₹4 crore a year earlier. Both have also built substantial order books totalling ₹64,000 crore, providing visibility into future demand. The question now is whether both these companies can sustain their recent profit growth as they ramp up production to meet hyperscaler demand. Although demand is currently concentrated in the US, India could become a major future growth driver as data centre projects by Meta and Reliance, Adani Group and Google scale up. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 HFCL: Hyperscaler Backlog and Backwards Integration HFCL Limited has established a strong position in the data centre and hyperscaler market. HFCL supplies optical connectivity products and passive infrastructure to several global hyperscalers and international networks. To capitalise on strong data centre demand, HFCL has developed a specialised product portfolio, including fibre, cabling and interconnect hardware. It designs high-density optical fibre cables to handle data traffic inside and between data centres. The cable line includes micro cables, ribbon cables, and intermittent bonded ribbon cables. Globally, demand for high-density cables is rising because of investments in artificial intelligence and the expansion of server racks. Order Book Dynamics: ₹28,911-Crore Backlog Anchored in AI Infrastructure HFCL's total confirmed order book reached ₹28,911 crore in Q2FY27. This backlog provides revenue visibility for the next 6-7 years. Optical fibre cables and data centre interconnects make up 64% of the company's total order book. Of the ₹18,500 crore export order book for cables and interconnects, about 70% comes from global hyperscalers. On the revenue side, data centre products and specialised connectivity solutions generate 65% to 75% of HFCL's product division revenue. Conventional telecommunications operators (telcos) accounted for the remaining 25%. Data centre connectivity products command higher prices and deliver higher operating margins than standard telecom infrastructure. Full-year FY27 connectivity revenue is projected at ₹800 crore, with management targeting ₹2,000 crore in FY28. A higher share of data centre solutions drove EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortisation) margin to 25.9% in Q2 FY27, up from 19.5% in Q2FY26. To meet hyperscalers' demand, HFCL is investing ₹1,800 crore across its manufacturing units. HFCL is investing ₹1,250 crore to build capacity of 600 metric tons (MT) per annum by October 2028. A preform is a silica glass rod that serves as the primary raw material for optical fibre. This in-house preform production will meet about 50% of HFCL’s internal fibre manufacturing requirements. The remaining half will come from multi-year contracts. Notably, preform prices surged by up to 600% due to market tightness. However, HFCL’s multi-month contracts (up to 24 months) keep unit costs predictable throughout their term. Current export demand is driven by North American hyperscalers. HFCL also expects demand to pick up from Europe, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East. India's data centre capacity is also projected to expand from 1.6 GW to 6-10 GW by 2030, supported by investments from major domestic conglomerates and government incentives. Earnings Acceleration: Q2 Net Profit Soars 448% to ₹394 Crore Consolidated revenue from operations grew 143.6% year-on-year to ₹2,541.8 crore in Q2FY27. This surge was fueled by accelerated deliveries to global hyperscalers and a 493% YoY surge in export revenue. EBITDA rose 223.6% to ₹658 crore, and margins expanded 640 basis points to 25.9%. Net profit grew 448.1% to ₹394.2 crore. Management has raised its FY27 revenue growth expectation to at least 80% year-on-year from the initial 20% target. It expects to reach its ₹10,000 crore annual revenue goal well before the original FY29 timeline. The company's total borrowings stood at ₹1,840.1 crore in H1FY27. Management plans to bring it down by FY28. docs.title: Down 30% and 37%: 2 fertiliser stocks betting on a new route to higher profits
docs.text: India’s fertiliser requirement rose to 677.18 lakh metric tonnes (LMT) in FY2025-26 from 649.43 LMT a year earlier, while imports of finished fertilisers reached 28.2 million tonnes worth more than US$14.5 billion. The wider import bill, including raw materials used in domestic production, exceeded US$27 billion. These figures expose a structural vulnerability: manufacturers can sell more fertiliser without gaining greater control over the inputs needed to produce it. For readers, Gujarat State Fertilizers & Chemicals (GSFC) and Rashtriya Chemicals and Fertilisers (RCF) offer two different ways to examine whether backward integration can improve manufacturing economics. The opportunity lies not simply in adding capacity, but in converting control over inputs, energy and production processes into lasting operating advantages. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now GSFC: From Fertiliser Production to a Chain of Linked Industrial Chemicals GSFC manufactures fertilisers and industrial chemicals. Its product portfolio includes agricultural nutrients and products used in industries such as textiles, engineering plastics, pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and surface coatings. Its portfolio includes caprolactam, Nylon-6, melamine, sulphuric acid, anhydrous ammonia and other chemical intermediates. This combination gives the company opportunities to use internally manufactured inputs across related production processes while selling chemicals into markets beyond agriculture. The Captive Chemical Chain: Where Integration Can Create Value GSFC's clearest example of backward integration is its production of hydroxylamine sulphate solution for captive use in caprolactam manufacturing. Caprolactam is an input for Nylon-6, which serves textile, industrial yarn and engineering-plastic markets. By operating across these stages, GSFC can participate in more than one part of the value chain. The advantage, however, depends on the economics of the chain. If the selling price of caprolactam falls relative to benzene and other production costs, margins can contract even when the company manufactures certain intermediates internally. During its February 2026 earnings call, management reported that the caprolactam–benzene spread had narrowed to US$495 per tonne from US$588 per tonne. This illustrates why integration should be assessed alongside product spreads, plant utilisation and the cost of externally purchased feedstock. Sulphuric Acid-V: A Commissioned Project With Two Potential Benefits GSFC commissioned its Sulphuric Acid-V project in January this year. The project adds sulphuric acid production capacity and generates steam that can be used at the company's Vadodara complex. Its potential benefits extend beyond replacing externally purchased acid. Captive acid availability can support the production of fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate and ammonium phosphate sulphate, while using generated steam elsewhere in the complex can improve energy utilisation. The key distinction is between installed capacity and realised savings. Readers need to establish how much additional acid is consumed internally, how much external procurement is displaced, and whether the steam generated reduces other energy costs. Sikka's Acid Plants: A New Step Towards Phosphatic Fertiliser Integration In October 2026, the GSFC board approved a phosphoric acid plant with a planned capacity of 600 metric tonnes per day (MTPD) and a sulphuric acid plant of 1,800 MTPD at its Sikka unit in Jamnagar, Gujarat. The proposal includes associated utilities and supporting infrastructure and is explicitly part of the company's backward integration strategy. Phosphoric acid and sulfuric acid are important inputs for phosphatic fertilisers and the project is of strategic importance. Production of these at Sikka could reduce GSFC’s dependence on purchased acid and also give it better control over the availability of inputs for its fertiliser operations. ALSO READIndia’s Rs 19,744 crore green hydrogen push has a fertiliser connection: 3 stocks to watch HX Sulphate Crystals: An Import-Substitution Proposal to Recheck GSFC commissioned its new 20 MTPD hydroxylamine sulphate crystal plant at Vadodara in October 2024. Built using in-house technology, the plant comprises two 10 MTPD production trains and expands GSFC’s capacity to serve demand for HX Crystal, a product used in agrochemical and pharmaceutical intermediates. The expansion supports import substitution and product-mix flexibility. In FY2025–26, GSFC reported record annual sales and export volumes for HX Crystal, indicating the product’s growing contribution to its industrial-products business. Melamine and Industrial Customers: Diversification Beyond Agriculture GSFC sells melamine under the Gujlamine brand. The chemical is used in laminates, plywood-related products, coatings and other industrial applications. Its published customer information includes names such as Century Laminates, Greenply Industries, Asian Paints and Kitply Industries among melamine customers. Other customer listings include businesses in automotive components and related industrial markets. These relationships show the breadth of GSFC's industrial reach. Q1FY27: Stronger Chemical Earnings, but Not Proof of a Permanent Advantage GSFC's Q1FY27 results provide a useful operating baseline before the next quarterly disclosure. Industrial products sales reached ₹635 crore, up 15% year on year, while segment earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) increased to ₹116 crore from ₹25 crore a year earlier. Management attributed the improvement mainly to higher caprolactam sales and a wider caprolactam–benzene spread, which increased to US$816 per tonne from US$540 per tonne. The figures show how the industrial chemical business can benefit when selling prices and feedstock economics move favourably. They do not establi

docs.title: Narayana Murthy’s family office bets Rs 310 cr on 2 new, beaten-down stocks
docs.text: Narayana Murthy Portfolio: Two New Bets on India's Building Boom Six months ago, the listed portfolio of Narayana Murthy's family office was a short, quiet list. Today it reads like the client roster of an engineering firm. Catamaran Ventures, the investment arm of the Infosys co-founder, has added six manufacturing names to its disclosed holdings in just two quarters. Eight of its nine listed stocks now make something you can touch, from forgings and alloy steel to aircraft parts and generators. The September 2026 shareholding filings add two more. Catamaran now holds 1.06% of Kirloskar Oil Engines, a stake worth about Rs 289 cr, and 1.05% of Ador Welding, worth about Rs 23 cr. That is a fresh commitment of over Rs 310 cr, and the Kirloskar stake alone is now one of the biggest in Catamaran's listed book. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Kirloskar Oil Engines now trades about 31% below its 52-week high, Ador Welding about 28%. Both companies have just reported thinner margins, and both blame costlier raw materials. So, is Murthy's office buying a passing dip in two businesses riding India's capex cycle, or stepping into a margin squeeze with further to run? The filings and the financials offer some clues. #1 Kirloskar Oil Engines: The Data Centre Power Stock in Murthy's Book Incorporated in 2009, Kirloskar Oil Engines (KOEL) took over the engine business of the Kirloskar group in a 2010 restructuring. With a market cap of Rs 26,088 cr, it makes generator sets from 1 kW to 10 MW, plus industrial engines for ships, defence, nuclear plants, railways and farms. It claims about 28% of India's generator set market. Catamaran holds 15,43,969 shares. At the closing price of Rs 1,869 on 22nd October 2026, that stake is worth close to Rs 289 cr. Holdings below 1% are not disclosed, so buying may have started earlier. From Farm Pumps to AI Data Centres: The 192 MW HyperNext Order Much of the rally rests on data centres. A data centre cannot go dark when the grid trips, so every server hall needs backup generators, and the big ones need dozens. On 19th June 2026, KOEL told the BSE it had won an order from HyperNext, a data centre developer, for 96 units of its 2,500 kVA Optiprime power systems, adding up to 192 MW. The company called it one of India's largest standby power deployments for data centres. The stock hit its 20% upper circuit on the next trading day. Management now wants KOEL to become a USD 2 billion revenue company by FY30, a little over twice its FY26 consolidated sales. The board has cleared Rs 2,100 cr of new capacity at its Kagal plant, of which Rs 1,400 cr is meant for large engines aimed at data centres and exports. Kirloskar Oil Engines Financials: 30% EBITDA Growth, With a Lender Inside A caution first. KOEL's consolidated accounts include Arka Fincap, its lending arm. That is why consolidated borrowings stood at Rs 5,374 cr in FY26, while the engine business on its own carried just Rs 131 cr. Of the Rs 523 cr of consolidated interest cost, only Rs 11 cr sits in the standalone business. Financial YearFY21FY22FY23FY24FY25FY265Y CAGRSales (Rs cr)3,2964,0225,0205,8986,3297,70118%EBITDA (Rs cr)3874127341,0271,1811,41430%Net Profit (Rs cr)19717133244047656223% Source: Screener.in EBITDA here refers to operating profit before other income. Since Arka's interest cost sits below the EBITDA line, that 30% flatters the factory. The standalone engine business grew sales at 16% a year from FY21 to FY26, operating profit at 21% and net profit at 22%. ALSO READ4x oil production target by FY30: An under-the-radar smallcap betting on bigger profits The latest quarter is where the worry sits. In Q1 FY27, standalone sales rose 16% to Rs 1,461 cr, but EBITDA fell 4% and the margin slipped to 11.2% from 13.5%. Management blamed weaker exports, higher commodity costs and a delay in passing on price hikes. Consolidated profit fell 17% to Rs 111 cr. Kirloskar Oil Engines Share Price: A 3x Swing in 12 Months The share price of Kirloskar Oil Engines has compounded at 53% a year over five years, as per Screener. In the past 12 months it went from a low of Rs 883 to a high of Rs 2,720, a little over three times, before closing at Rs 1,869 on 22nd October 2026. After the fall, it still trades at a PE of about 46x against a current industry median of about 38x, and at 7 times book value. The 10-year median PE for the company is 23x while the industry median for the same period is 34x. Its larger rival, Cummins India, trades at about 49x. Promoters hold 41.03%, domestic institutions 27.04% and foreign investors 11.06%. Retail has piled in too. The number of shareholders rose from 68,891 in December 2023 to 1,28,854 in September 2026. Margin Squeeze and the Rs 2,100 Crore Kagal Bet: What Could Go Wrong Three things need watching. Margins, because another quarter near 11% would test a 46x multiple, and Q2 FY27 numbers are due in the coming weeks. Execution, because Rs 2,100 cr of capex is a big cheque for a business that earned Rs 461 cr of standalone profit in FY26. And competition, because in data centre gensets KOEL is the challenger, not the incumbent, and big orders tend to be lumpy. #2 Ador Welding: A 75-Year-Old Welding Stock at 18x Earnings Incorporated in 1951, Ador Welding is one of India's oldest welding companies. With a market cap of Rs 2,211 cr, it makes welding electrodes, wires, fluxes, machines and automation systems from five plants, with capacity for 90,000 tonnes of consumables and 30,000 welding machines a year. Catamaran holds 1,82,798 shares, or 1.05%, worth about Rs 23 cr at Rs 1,270. That is a starter-sized position, roughly one-twelfth of what it has put into Kirloskar Oil Engines. Why Every Bridge, Pipeline and Factory Needs a Welder Almost everything India is building, from bridges and pipelines to ships, power plants and factory sheds, is held together by a weld.

docs.title: Rs 1,053 cr order book, 22.9% ROCE: An under-the-radar smallcap eyes the data centre boom
docs.text: India's data centre boom is creating an unusual opportunity for businesses that have little to do with computers. Every new facility needs a building and the more complex the facility becomes, the more demanding its structural requirements can be. Steel manufacturers capable of supplying specialised structures could benefit from a construction market that is attracting billions of dollars in investment. There is, however, a catch. Being present in a fast-growing market does not automatically make a company a good investment. The real test is whether it can win orders at attractive prices, deliver them without cost overruns and collect its money without tying up too much capital. M & B Engineering 1-Year Share Price Chart Source: Screener.in This is what makes M&B Engineering interesting. The company has capabilities in pre-engineered buildings, heavy structural steel and self-supported roofing systems and it is investing in additional capacity to address more complex construction projects. Its opportunity is to move beyond conventional industrial buildings into specialised structures, including data centres, while maintaining the profitability of its existing business. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Beyond Conventional Warehouses: The Structural Demands of Data Centre A data centre is not an ordinary warehouse. It must support heavy equipment, meet demanding structural specifications and accommodate complex layouts. Developers also want these facilities completed quickly, because delays can push back the start of commercial operations. Pre-engineered buildings (PEBs) offer one way to speed up construction. Much of the structure is designed and manufactured before it reaches the site, reducing the work required there. Heavy structural steel serves buildings that need greater load-bearing strength and more complex designs. M&B operates through two divisions. Phenix handles PEBs and heavy structural steel, while Proflex specialises in self-supported steel roofing systems. In Q1FY27, Phenix generated Rs 214 crore in revenue, up 22% year on year, while Proflex contributed Rs 77 crore, up 25%. Phenix accounted for roughly 74% of quarterly revenue, making it the company's larger business. The margin problem behind the growth story Financial indicatorFY26Q1FY27What it tells investorsRevenue growth (YoY)27.4%22.5%Growth remains strongOperating margin11.3%11.4% EBITDA marginQuarterly margin remains below the year-ago levelYear-ago operating EBITDA marginNot comparable on this basis14.2%A 2.8 percentage-point decline year on year Source: M&B Engineering FY26 results and Q1FY27 investor presentation. The proposed investment in heavy structural steel is therefore an expansion of an existing capability, not a bet on an entirely unfamiliar market. The question is whether data centres and other specialised projects can provide an additional source of growth without squeezing margins further. Management estimates that steel-intensive construction could represent a US$12-14 billion opportunity in India's data centre market over the next five years. These estimates point to the scale of the potential market, not the revenue available to M&B. Steel construction accounts for only around 8-10% of a data centre's total investment, with civil works and mechanical, electrical and plumbing requirements accounting for the rest, according to management. M&B will capture only a fraction of the steel opportunity, depending on the projects it wins and the value of the structures it supplies. The opportunity is real, but the size of the market alone tells investors very little. What matters is whether M&B can win enough orders at attractive margins to turn this potential demand into profitable growth. The Sanand Expansion: A Rs 30 Crore CAPEX Bet on 22,000-Tonne Capacity M&B is investing to capture this opportunity. In August 2026, its board approved Rs 30 crore for a fully automated heavy structural steel processing line at Sanand. The investment will increase annual capacity from 12,000 tonnes to 22,000 tonnes, with operations expected to begin in Q1FY28. The line is aimed at data centres, high-rise buildings and other complex structures. The company is also adding 20,000 tonnes of annual PEB capacity at Sanand, taking it from 72,000 tonnes to 92,000 tonnes after commissioning in October 2026. A further 20,000-tonne expansion at Cheyyar is targeted for completion in Q3FY28, taking total PEB and structural steel capacity to approximately 1,54,000 tonnes annually. For a company of M&B's size, these are significant additions. But capacity creates value only when customers use it. If orders arrive slowly or pricing weakens, the new facilities could add costs without delivering the expected returns. Ultimately, utilization, product mix and margins will determine whether this expansion pays off. ALSO READ‘Data centre in a container’: The multibillion-dollar opportunity and 2 stocks to watch Q1FY27 Financials: 22.5% Revenue Growth Masked by a 2.8% EBITDA Drop The company's financial performance offers a useful starting point for assessing its expansion plans. Consolidated revenue rose 27.4% in FY26, but the operating profit margin fell from 12.8% in FY25 to 11.3% in FY26. The latest quarter showed a similar trend. Revenue grew 22.5% year on year in Q1FY27, while the operating EBITDA margin declined to 11.4% from 14.2% a year earlier. Management attributed the pressure partly to higher freight costs on shipments to the US and increased inland transportation costs there. Geopolitical uncertainty surrounding West Asia added to the strain. The company expects lower US Section 232 duties, higher export revenue and additional capacity to support a gradual margin recovery, particularly in the second half of FY27. docs.title: Margins to recover to 5.8% by Q4: IDFC FIRST Bank CEO
docs.text: IDFC FIRST Bank expects credit and deposit growth to remain around 20% in the near term, says MD & CEO V Vaidyanathan. He tells Christina Titus that the impact of the proposed changes in insurance commission norms will be largely offset by savings from FCNR(B) funding and the benefits of higher interest rates. Excerpts: ALSO READIDFC FIRST Bank Q2 results: Profit after tax jumps 196.5% YoY to Rs 1,045 crore The bank reported a 196.5% year-on-year increase in net profit in Q2. What were the key drivers? Our growth has been steady, with the core loan book and deposits expanding by around 20-22%. More importantly, operating expenses are growing about 500 basis points slower than income, reflecting tighter cost controls. This has helped operating profit grow 39%. At the same time, credit costs, or provisions, have declined 27% year-on-year as portfolio quality improves. Higher operating profit, coupled with lower provisions, is driving profitability. Do you expect credit and deposit growth to sustain at these levels? We believe growth of around 20% in both loans and deposits is sustainable for the foreseeable future, given the demand environment. We are still a relatively young bank with a smaller base, making growth of around 20% quite comfortable for us. How have FCNR(B) deposits affected margins? What is your outlook for net interest margins? The decline in net interest margin (NIM) is partly optical. We raised loans worth $2.5 billion through our International Banking Unit to lend to NRI customers, enabling them to place FCNR(B) deposits with the bank. This expanded the denominator without a corresponding increase in net interest income. However, the larger denominator also proportionately benefits the operating expense and credit cost ratios. Looking at NIM alone does not capture the full picture, which becomes evident at the return-on-assets (RoA) level. We expect margins to recover to around 5.8% by Q4 FY27 as the excess liquidity from FCNR(B) deposits is deployed. These inflows have been hugely positive for the bank, providing substantial structural liquidity for three to five years. Have deficient monsoons and drought-like conditions in some states affected your loan portfolio? Based on what we see today, we remain comfortable with our credit cost outlook for Q3 and Q4. However, the situation is evolving, and we are monitoring developments very closely. How do you see rural lending evolving amid these risks? Could weak monsoons and rising inflation hurt rural consumption and credit growth? Rural financing is an integral part of the country's economic ecosystem, and credit must continue to flow to these segments. We will continue expanding our rural loan portfolio across microfinance, tractor loans, Kisan Credit Cards, dairy loans, rural SME loans and micro-enterprise lending. I do not necessarily expect rural consumption to slow. The impact of the monsoon has not been uniform across the country, and several regions have received normal rainfall. ALSO READCreditAccess Grameen posts four-fold jump in profit What impact do you expect from the insurance regulator's proposed commission norms? How will the bank absorb the potential hit to fee income? We should assume the draft regulations are implemented in their current form and factor in the impact. However, there are offsets. The Rs 35,000 crore raised through FCNR(B) deposits has come at a cost roughly 1 percentage point lower than comparable domestic funding. This translates into significant savings on funding costs. Further, if interest rates rise in line with our house view, our floating-rate loan book will reprice faster, while deposit rates will adjust with a lag. These benefits should largely offset the impact of the proposed commission norms, allowing the bank to broadly meet its profitability targets for FY28.

docs.title: Average balance in PMJDY accounts touches a record Rs 5,438
docs.text: The average balance in no-frills bank accounts under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) has hit a new high of Rs 5,438 after fresh accretion of around Rs 7,000 crore in less than two months. These accounts now hold cumulative deposits of around Rs 3.24 lakh crore as of October 14, up from Rs 3.17 lakh crore on August 19, 2026. As a result, the average balance rose from Rs 5,356 to a new record of Rs 5,438. The average deposit has risen consistently — from Rs 3,449 in March 2021. ALSO READKarnataka, Keralam, Assam report strong capex in H1 The number of PMJDY accounts has also grown, reaching 595.9 million, up from 590.9 million about two months back. Public sector banks continue to dominate the scheme, accounting for nearly 77% of beneficiaries and deposits. Public sector banks had 458.4 million beneficiaries and deposits of Rs 2.52 lakh crore. Regional rural banks (RRBs) accounted for another 111.8 million beneficiaries, with deposits of Rs 61,311 crore. Private sector banks had 23.8 million beneficiaries and deposits of Rs 10,265 crore, while rural cooperative banks accounted for 1.9 million beneficiaries. The distribution of accounts underscores the importance of rural banking infrastructure in expanding access to formal financial services. Of the total beneficiaries, 462.7 million were associated with rural and semi-urban bank branches, compared with 133.2 million at urban and metropolitan branches. Rural and semi-urban beneficiaries thus accounted for around 78% of the total, reflecting the scheme’s focus on extending banking access beyond major urban centres. Women accounted for 332.3 million beneficiaries, or nearly 56% of the total. This points to the scheme’s role in expanding women’s access to formal banking and strengthening their participation in the financial system. Banks had issued 417.9 million RuPay debit cards to beneficiaries, equivalent to around 70% of the total beneficiary base. The gap between beneficiary numbers and cards issued indicates scope to deepen the use of digital payment facilities and formal banking services. ALSO READOctober PMI rises to 56.7; Input cost inflation eased, manufacturing strong The trinity of Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and mobile (JAM) has played a key role in enabling large-scale, technology-driven, real-time direct benefit transfers (DBTs), especially during the Covid-19 pandemic. Between FY15 and FY24, direct benefit transfers have generated cumulative savings of nearly Rs 5.14 lakh crore. PMJDY accounts require no minimum balance and offer interest on deposits, making them both accessible and appealing for low-income households. These accounts are eligible for direct benefit transfer (DBT), Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana, Atal Pension Yojana, and Micro Units Development & Refinance Agency Bank (MUDRA) scheme.

 Here's why Choice Broking is cautiously positive on Chennai Petroleum and ASK Automotive; bearish on PNB Housing Finance. (Photo: Shutterstock.com)

Sachin Gupta, VP – Research, Choice Broking Buy CHENNPETRO in cash at ₹1,475 | SL ₹1,430 | TGT ₹1,570 CHENNPETRO is showing signs of recovery after recent volatility, closing at ₹1,475.60 on Friday. The stock is sustaining above its 50-day EMA and the middle Bollinger Band near ₹1,446.90, while trading comfortably above the 200-day EMA, indicating a positive broader trend. The RSI at 52.95 suggests improving momentum, although bullish strength is yet to gain traction. The immediate support zone is placed at ₹1,430–₹1,380, while a sustained move above ₹1,475, backed by strong volumes, could trigger further upside. Overall, the outlook remains cautiously positive as long as the stock holds above its key moving averages. CHECK Stock Market LIVE Updates Buy ASKAUTOLTD in cash around ₹540-550 | SL ₹527 | TGT ₹565/580 ASK Automotive has witnessed a sharp correction from its recent peak of ₹688.60 and is currently showing signs of stabilisation near ₹550.75. After the recent decline, the stock is approaching a crucial support zone of ₹527–₹532, where the 50 per cent Fibonacci retracement level at ₹531.95 coincides with the rising 200-day EMA at ₹527.86. This confluence makes the zone important for a potential recovery. If the stock manages to hold above this support, a technical bounce towards ₹569, followed by ₹596, could be on the cards. However, a sustained recovery is needed to improve the near-term price structure, while a decisive breakdown below ₹527 could extend the correction towards the next support near ₹495. Sell PNBHOUSING Futures ₹1,090 | SL ₹1,140 | TGT ₹1,040/1,000 PNBHOUSING has turned weak on the daily chart after breaking below the lower trendline of a multi-month ascending channel. The stock declined sharply by 4.34 per cent to ₹1,089.10, with rising selling pressure supporting the breakdown. It has also slipped below its key moving average and the middle Bollinger Band, indicating continued weakness in the near-term trend. The RSI at 39.12 further points to declining momentum. Considering the current chart structure, traders may look for short-selling opportunities in the ₹1,090–1,100 range, with a stop-loss at ₹1,140 and downside targets of ₹1,040 and ₹1,000.

As highlighted in our previous weekly outlook, the Nifty had entered oversold territory following the recent sharp correction, creating the possibility of a technical rebound. However, despite intermittent recovery attempts and buying interest at lower levels, the index failed to sustain its upward momentum and faced selling pressure near the 23,200 resistance level. Global uncertainties, particularly concerns surrounding the sharp rise in Brent crude oil prices and escalating geopolitical tensions, continued to weigh on market sentiment. The possibility of crude oil prices exceeding $110 per barrel has further intensified concerns about inflation and its potential impact on the Indian equity market. Ganesh Dongre, AVP — Equity Research at Anand Rathi, believes the Indian stock market mood is cautious after a continuous slide in the Nifty 50 index despite being in the oversold zone. Speaking on the outlook for the Nifty 50 index, Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said, the 50-stock index witnessed profit booking near the 23,200 mark and ended the week around the crucial support zone of 22,500–22,600. This zone remains significant, as it represents an important historical support area near previous yearly and quarterly lows. “On the upside, the immediate resistance is placed in the 23,200–23,400 range, followed by the 24,100–24,200 zone, where the 200-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) is positioned. A sustained weekly close above 23,200–23,400 would improve the near-term technical outlook and could pave the way for a recovery towards 24,000–24,200,” said Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi. The Anand Rathi expert said that on the downside, the 22,500–22,200 range will remain an important support zone in the coming week. A decisive breakdown below this range could revive selling pressure and drag the index towards its previous low and support of 21700-22,000. On the outlook for the Bank Nifty index, Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said, the immediate support for the key benchmark index is around 53,500, which corresponds to the recent weekly low, while the next important support stands near 53,000. A sustained breakdown below 53,000 could weaken the technical structure further and trigger renewed selling pressure. On the upside, the immediate resistance zone is placed around 56,400–56,500, where the 200-day EMA is positioned. A decisive, sustained breakout above 56,500 would strengthen the near-term technical outlook and could open the door to a further recovery. On the Indian stock market outlook and key levels regarding Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty, Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi said, “Overall, both the Nifty and Bank Nifty remain in a cautious technical phase following the recent correction. For the market to establish a meaningful recovery, the Nifty needs to reclaim and sustain above the 23,200–23,400 resistance zone, while the Bank Nifty must move decisively above 56,400–56,500 to improve its technical outlook.” Regarding stocks to buy on Monday , Ganesh Dongre of Anand Rathi recommended these three shares: Eternal , Bank of Baroda , and Apollo Hospitals Enterprises. 1] Eternal: Buy in ₹ 315 to ₹ 320 range | Target ₹ 330 | Stop Loss ₹ 305; 2] Bank of Baroda (BoB): Buy in ₹ 230 to ₹ 233 range | Target ₹ 242 | Stop Loss ₹ 225; and 3] Apollo Hospitals Enterprises: Buy in ₹ 7700 to ₹ 7730 range | Target ₹ 8100 | Stop Loss ₹ 7550. docs.title: Buy JSW Steel Ltd For Target Rs.1,470 by Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd
docs.text:
Earnings beat driven by strong volume; outlook robust Consolidated performance 
* Since BPSL has been de-consolidated w.e.f. Mar’26 end, the YoY financials are not comparable. Comparing with adjusted ex-BPSL pro forma for 2QFY26, the 2QFY27 revenue stood at INR545b (vs. our est. INR486b), up 31% YoY and 15% QoQ, driven by strong volume growth.
* Adj. EBITDA stood at INR99.4b (+39% YoY and +6% QoQ, comparing with ex-BPSL pro forma), which came in above our estimates mainly due to higher-than-expected volume. Adj. EBITDA/t was in line at INR13,326/t (+24% YoY, ex-BPSL pro forma), down 11% QoQ, due to higher coking coal prices and lower realizations.
* APAT stood at INR51b (+10% QoQ) vs. our est. of INR33.1b. The beat was mainly driven by higher-than-expected operating performance and lower interest costs due to lower debt and interest rates.
* Consolidated 2Q production stood at 7.27mt (+5% YoY and +10% QoQ) on account of Vijayanagar BF-3 ramp-up. Sales volume stood at 7.46mt, and comparing with adjusted ex-BPSL pro forma for 2QFY26, volume grew 13% YoY and 19% QoQ during the quarter.
* Consol. ASP stood at INR73,000/t (vs. INR75,780/t in 1QFY27 and INR62,640/t (ex-BPSL) in 2QFY26), mainly driven by steel price recovery.
* Net debt-to-EBITDA stood at 1.28x in 2QFY27 vs. 1.46x in 1QFY27. Net debt as of Sep’26 stood at INR445b, down by INR16.8b QoQ.
 Highlights from the management commentary 
* Management expects steel volumes to increase in 3QFY27, driven by full production from Vijayanagar BF3. The company is on track to achieve its FY27 production and sales guidance.
* Steel prices recovered by 2Q end as monsoon conditions eased and construction activity improved. Management indicated that the Oct’26 price hikes, along with the price recovery during Aug-Sep’26, will reflect in 3Q realizations.
* Coking coal costs increased by ~USD10/t in 2QFY27 against the earlier guidance of USD12-15/t. Management expects coking coal costs to increase by ~USD25/t in 3QFY27.
* Iron ore costs were slightly higher in 2QFY27, due to supply constraints, including disruptions at NMDC's Chhattisgarh mines and monsoon-related logistical issues in Central India and Odisha. Management expects costs to remain marginally higher in 3QFY27, while domestic iron ore prices could soften over coming quarters as supply bottlenecks ease and domestic prices catch up with international prices.
* Management revised its capex pipeline from ~INR1.3t to INR1.48t, to be deployed over the next 5-6 years.
* JSTL delivered better-than-expected earnings in 2Q, supported by strong volume growth owing to Vijaynagr ramp-up. We remain constructive on the company's medium-term outlook, underpinned by the commissioning and ramp-up of new capacities, robust domestic steel demand, and rising share of VAP. In addition, enhancing captive iron ore and improving coal security should strengthen cost competitiveness and support margin expansion.
* We maintain our FY27/28 earnings estimates, factoring in sales volume of +30mt by FY28E, driven by the ramp-up of new capacity. Despite input cost volatility, we believe EBITDA/t will rebound to ~INR14,000/t by FY28E on account of domestic steel price recovery.
* With the transfer of BPSL to JFE JV via a slump sale, the company’s consolidated debt has declined significantly to INR445b as of Sep’26. This translates to a net debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 1.28x in 2QFY27. The sharp deleveraging has strengthened JSTL’s balance sheet, unlocking future capex plans.
* At CMP, JSTL trades at 6.9x FY28E EV/EBITDA. We largely retain our FY28 earnings estimate and reiterate our BUY rating on the stock with a TP of INR1,460, valued on SoTP basis.

docs.title: Best auto stocks to buy ahead of Diwali 2026: Nuvama bets big on Eicher Motors, Hyundai and Tata Motors PV - Here's why
docs.text:
Initial festive-season registrations since Navratri have been mixed. Commercial vehicle (CV) registrations grew 21% year-on-year (YoY), while two-wheeler (2W) registrations rose 13%. Passenger vehicle (PV) registrations, however, declined 9% YoY. Festive-season performance has also lagged the over 20% growth recorded across categories in the first half of FY27. Dealer checks across Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand indicate moderating demand due to a high base following last year's GST cuts, intermittent weakness in rural demand, and longer waiting periods, particularly for passenger vehicles. Meanwhile, electric vehicle (EV) adoption continues to grow at a robust double-digit pace across segments. Among two-wheelers, TVS Motor and Honda have gained market share, while Bajaj Auto, Hero MotoCorp and Eicher Motors have lost share. Nuvama attributed Eicher Motors' share loss to waiting periods for key models, including the Bullet 350 and Classic 350. The brokerage's dealer survey indicates that a Madhya Pradesh Honda dealer expects growth of 3–5% during September–November 2026, compared with 10% in the first half of FY27, citing slower rural demand amid deficient rainfall and lower crop realisations. A Bihar dealer expects Honda's two-wheeler sales to grow 15–18% during the festive period, below the 24% growth recorded between April and August 2026. For Hero MotoCorp, a Jharkhand dealer expects festive-season growth of 10%, compared with 12% in the first half of FY27. Rural demand is likely to remain healthy in the state due to normal rainfall. Nuvama's checks with passenger-vehicle dealers in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar also indicate uneven festive demand. A Bihar-based Maruti Suzuki dealer expects growth of 18% during September–November 2026, compared with 8% between April and August. The dealer reported a one-month waiting period for the Brezza and Fronx, along with a low inventory of around 20 days. In contrast, a Hyundai dealer in Madhya Pradesh expects muted growth during the festive season, compared with 10% growth in the first half of FY27. Nuvama said new launches, including the Bayon, could support volumes, with the model carrying a waiting period of around one month. Meanwhile, EV demand remains resilient. An Ather Energy dealer in Madhya Pradesh reported waiting periods of 30 days for the Rizta model and 15 days for the Konarc, although growth could remain moderate until supplies improve in the fourth quarter of FY27.
